Your seal
In your life you saw {0}. Scholars today still argue about what they meant.
You yourself were one of those who adapted.
The rains that changed
For three years the river has not spilled over its banks, and the winter wheat comes up thin. A stranger from the east says his people now sow millet and rice in the summer rains instead.

Studies of seeds from excavated sites suggest that as the monsoon weakened, many Indus villagers grew more summer crops that cope better with drought, such as millets and rice. Small villages that adapted survived, while the great cities, which depended on surplus grain and long-distance trade, slowly emptied.
Try millet as the stranger says
The first year your father grumbles that millet is bird food. The second year it is what keeps the house alive.
Keep to the wheat your grandparents grew
The rains fail again, and the granary is empty before the new season comes.
Move closer to a river that still runs
You leave the house your grandfather built, but the new place still has water.

The Indus cities did not fall in a day. The monsoon weakened and the rivers shifted slowly over centuries, so slowly that hardly anyone saw a "collapse" within one life, only a little less rain, one more dry well. Those who adapted, changing crops, moving, splitting into small villages, survived and became ancestors of South Asians today. What vanished was the great system built for the old world: the cities, the seals and the writing. Scholars still argue how much nature was to blame, but the lesson still holds for a world whose climate is changing today.
Each year a little less rain, one more dry well. If you knew the world would keep slowly changing through your grandchildren’s lives, what would you teach them?
One of your children falls ill and dies. The family lays the little body in a clay jar and buries it beneath the floor.

Knossos was the largest Minoan palace, with hundreds of rooms around a central court and no fortress walls. Arthur Evans excavated it from 1900 and named the culture “Minoan” after King Minos of Greek legend. We do not know what the Cretans called themselves.

Akrotiri on Thera (Santorini) was a harbour town with houses of two or three storeys and brightly painted walls. The island’s volcano erupted and buried it in ash. Unlike Pompeii, no bodies have been found, so the people probably escaped first.

Mycenae was a hilltop citadel with walls of such huge stones that later Greeks believed the giant Cyclopes had built them. Heinrich Schliemann excavated it in 1876 and found a gold mask he called the “Mask of Agamemnon”, but it is centuries older than any possible Trojan War.

Pylos was a palace in western Greece. When it burned around 1180 BCE, the fire baked more than a thousand clay tablets in its archive hard, so they survived. They tell us how the palace counted sheep, handed out rations, and what it feared in its last year.

Ugarit was one of the busiest ports of the eastern Mediterranean, with merchants from Egypt, the Hittite lands, Cyprus and Greece, and a new cuneiform alphabet of only 30 letters, one of the world’s first alphabets. It was destroyed around 1190 BCE and never rebuilt, until a farmer ploughing his field broke into a tomb in 1928.

Cyprus was the great copper source of the age, probably the land called “Alashiya” in letters of the time. Copper was cast into ingots shaped like an ox-hide, weighing about 20–30 kilograms, and shipped all over the sea, since bronze needed copper mixed with tin at about ten to one.

Most people of this age did not live in palaces but in villages of farmers and shepherds, growing barley, olives and grapes and sending part of their harvest to the palace. These villages were what carried on after the palaces fell.

The Minoans’ Linear A script still cannot be read. The Mycenaeans’ Linear B was deciphered in 1952 and records thousands of ordinary people’s names, but mostly as entries in palace accounts. So in this game you have only a nickname.

Linear B tablets show that the Mycenaean palaces organised work in great detail, with dozens of named trades: bronze-smiths, oil-boilers, weavers, grinders, counters of sheep. The palace handed out raw materials and food rations. Of the Minoan age we know far less, because their script still cannot be read.
a palace family close to the king (the wanax)

Linear B tablets at Pylos list hundreds of women and their children by task, such as grinding grain and spinning, with rations of grain and figs. Many are named after lands across the sea to the east and may have been captives or slaves. The tablets use do-e-ro for slave and wa-na-ka (wanax) for king.
woollen cloth
perfumed oil
The winter rains are thin this year, and the barley comes up patchy.
The rains come on time, and the olive trees are heavy with fruit.

Around the Aegean most rain falls in winter and summers are dry, so farmers grew barley, olives and vines, which cope with drought. Tree rings in Anatolia and falling Dead Sea levels suggest a severe dry spell around 1200 BCE, though how severe and how long is still debated.
There is no palace left to keep accounts for, and no one needs a scribe. You write your name in the dirt and rub it out.

After the palaces fell, Linear B vanished from Greece entirely. The Greeks had no writing for some 400 years, until they adopted the Phoenician letters around 800 BCE, which became the Greek alphabet still used today.
Wrote your first clay tablet

For days the ground shakes hard, and the whole town takes to the boats and flees to Crete. A few days later the volcano at the heart of Thera explodes. The sky goes dark at noon and ash falls on the sea like snow. The town you were born in disappears under metres of dust.

The eruption of Thera was one of the largest in human history. Its date is still argued over: radiocarbon points to around 1600 BCE or a little earlier, while comparing pottery with Egypt points to around 1500 BCE. No bodies have been found at Akrotiri; most scholars think the townspeople were warned by earthquakes and left first.
Escaped the eruption of Thera
The northern sky turns black and a boom rolls across the sea. Grey ash falls on the fields, and a great wave smashes the boats on the north coast.

Ash from Thera has been found on Crete and as far as Anatolia, and tsunami deposits on Crete’s north coast. But the Minoans did not collapse at once: their palaces went on for decades, perhaps a century.
Many palaces on Crete are burned. Knossos survives, but the people in the palace now speak a new tongue from the mainland, and the scribes begin to write a new script.

Around 1450 BCE most Minoan palaces were destroyed. Knossos seems to have come under Mycenaeans from the mainland, and Linear B, used to write an early form of Greek, replaced Linear A. The cause is still debated: invasion, earthquakes or conflict within.
Builders haul stones bigger than a house to make the citadel gate, and above it carve two lions facing a column.

The Lion Gate of Mycenae was built around 1250 BCE, one of the oldest large sculptures in Europe. Around the same time several Greek citadels thickened their walls and secured water inside them, as if preparing for something.
Survived the day the city burned
Smoke rises from the harbour. Dozens of strange ships are drawn up on the beach. People run for the hills, and that night the whole city burns.
Ugarit was destroyed around 1190 BCE. Arrowheads lie scattered in its streets, and no one ever rebuilt the city.
Fire sweeps through the palace in the night. The roof falls into the oil stores and the flames roar higher. By morning only blackened walls are left.
The palace of Pylos burned around 1180 BCE and was never rebuilt. The fire that destroyed it baked the clay tablets in its archive as hard as tile, so the palace’s last year of accounts survives.
Fire takes many houses inside the citadel. No one knows who set it: some say enemies, some say the townspeople themselves.
Mycenae was damaged by an earthquake around 1250 BCE and burned around 1190 BCE. Who or what caused it is unknown. People lived on there for a while, but there was no palace any more.
The palace of Knossos empties room by room. The stores are bare and no ships come from the mainland. Many families move high into the mountains, where no enemy can reach them.
At this time many Cretans moved to high mountain villages that were easy to defend, such as Karphi at more than 1,100 metres. Archaeologists call them “refuge settlements”.
The palace scribes no longer come for the harvest. Word comes that the palace has burned. For the first time the village keeps all its grain, but there is no one to trade with either.

When the palaces fell, the system of collecting produce and handing it back went with them. Villages that fed themselves carried on, but the craftsmen, scribes and merchants who depended on the palace lost their work overnight.
Sailors fleeing from the south say the pharaoh of Egypt has beaten the “Sea Peoples” at the mouth of the Nile and carved the battle on a temple wall.

Ramesses III carved his battle against the “Sea Peoples” on his temple at Medinet Habu around 1177 BCE. The name “Sea Peoples” was coined by modern scholars. They were probably many groups: pirates, mercenaries and whole families fleeing drought and war. One group, the Peleset, were probably the Philistines of the Bible.
No one builds big stone houses any more. There are fewer people in the village every year, and the pots are plainer; no one paints them as finely as in your grandparents’ day.

After the palaces fell, Greece’s population probably dropped sharply. Villages became smaller and farther apart, and long-distance trade almost stopped. Yet in this time iron began to spread: iron ore was easier to find than tin, so it did not depend on trade routes across the sea.
You help carry oil jars onto the ships and are paid in barley and figs.

There were no coins yet. Palaces gathered produce and handed it back as rations, while sea trade was weighed in copper, silver or gold. A ship that sank off Uluburun in Turkey around 1300 BCE carried about 10 tons of copper and about 1 ton of tin, enough for some 11 tons of bronze, along with glass ingots, ivory and jewellery from many lands.

Help your mother leave clay figures at the shrine
Plough for barley and tend the olive grove
Pick up fallen olives under the trees
Drive the sheep and goats up the hills
Look after the lambs

Build stone walls and mend the house
Trade at the harbour
Listen to the singer’s tales of heroes
Listen to grandmother’s tale of the monster in the labyrinth
Leaping the bull
In the great court of the palace, a young athlete grabs the horns of a charging bull and somersaults over its back to land on the far side. The crowd roars.

A wall painting at Knossos shows people leaping over a bull’s back. Scholars still argue whether this was a sport, a ritual or an imagined scene, and whether it could really be done. Later Greeks told of the Minotaur, half man and half bull, in a labyrinth beneath Knossos ✦, a legend written down nearly a thousand years after the Minoans.
Practise leaping a calf at home
The calf tosses its head and you land with a broken arm, but the village talks about it for years.
You clear it once, and then the calf chases you all round the yard.
Ask why it has to be a bull
Grandmother says the bull is the strength of the earth, which makes the ground shake when it is angry.
The saffron crocus
In autumn the village girls climb the rocky slopes to pick the red threads from saffron flowers one by one into little baskets.
A wall painting at Akrotiri shows girls gathering saffron. Saffron dyed cloth and may have been used as medicine. The paintings of Thera survived because volcanic ash buried them.
Pick until the basket is full
Your fingers are stained orange for days.
Chase the wild goats on the slope
A wild goat with long curved horns bounds from rock to rock far faster than you.
The Mistress of the Labyrinth
Your mother takes a jar of honey to the palace as an offering. A scribe writes on a clay tablet: “to the Mistress of the Labyrinth”.

A Linear B tablet from Knossos records an offering of honey to “da-pu-ri-to-jo po-ti-ni-ja”, usually read as “the Mistress of the Labyrinth”. The word labyrinth may come from labrys, the double axe that was a sacred Minoan symbol, but this is debated.
Ask where the labyrinth is
The scribe laughs and waves at the palace around you, with its hundreds of rooms.
Sneak a taste of the honey
Your mother catches you, but does not tell the scribe.
The boar’s-tusk helmet
Your uncle is sewing rows of boar tusks onto a leather cap. He says it takes the tusks of some forty boars to make a single helmet.
Boar’s-tusk helmets have been found in many Mycenaean tombs, and Homer describes one in the Iliad, composed some 500 years later. Some memories of this age were passed down in song for centuries.
Ask to go on the boar hunt
A boar charges and gashes your leg.
You come back with a pair of tusks, and your uncle sews them on the front of the helmet.
Try the helmet on
It is so heavy you can hardly lift your head.
The scribe’s pupil
A palace scribe needs a pupil. He says you must learn nearly a hundred signs, each one a syllable, and write fast before the clay dries.
Linear A, the Minoan script, survives on more than a thousand tablets and objects, but it still cannot be read because we do not know the language.

Linear B has about 90 syllable signs plus pictures for goods. In 1952 Michael Ventris, an English architect, showed it was an early form of Greek, building on the work of Alice Kober. The tablets were not meant to last; they survived because the fires that burned the palaces baked them hard.
By the end of the first year you can count the sheep for him.
Keep helping at home
Your family is glad of the help.
The wide sea
A ship’s master needs young hands to row and bail. The ship will go to Cyprus and Egypt and be back before the winter winds.

Ships of this age used both sail and oars, mostly hugged the coast, and went to sea only in the calmer summer months. Sea trade tied Egypt, the Hittites, Cyprus, Ugarit, Crete and Greece together, so tightly that some historians call it “the first globalisation”.
Go with the ship
A storm drives the ship onto rocks. You swim ashore but lose everything you had.
You see the pyramids from afar and come home with blue glass beads.
You listen to the sailors’ tales when they return.
The wedding
The two families talk of marrying you to the child of a shepherd from the next village.
We know little about marriage in this age directly: the tablets are palace accounts, not private letters. Most of what we know comes from family tombs used for generations.
The wedding has honey bread and wine, and a singer tells stories late into the night.
Ask to wait a year
Both families grumble, but agree to wait.
The shaking ground
The ground shakes every month. Walls crack all over town and the wells smell of sulphur. Some old people say it is time to move to Crete.

At Akrotiri there are signs that people were repairing earthquake damage and had stacked belongings in the streets before the town was buried. Many scholars think only a few years passed between the great earthquake and the eruption.
Move to Crete now
Left Thera before the eruption
You load the whole house onto a boat. The neighbours laugh. A year later they row after you with nothing in their hands.
Stay and repair the house
You replaster the wall and paint lilies on it.
The palace sheep
A palace scribe comes to count the sheep. He says this year you must hand over the wool he has written down, and if you fall short your name will be written as “still owing”.
The Knossos tablets record tens of thousands of sheep with each shepherd and the wool each was due to deliver. When someone fell short, the scribe wrote o-pe-ro, “owing” or “lacking”.
Deliver it all, even if your family is left short
Your name is written as complete, and no one asks anything more.
Hide some sheep up in the hills
The palace herdsmen find the hidden sheep, and you are written down as owing for two more years.
Your family has wool enough to weave for the winter.
The rations
Every month the women of the palace grinding room line up for rations of wheat and figs; children get half. This year the scribe says the palace is short of grain.
Give part of your share to your children
You grow thinner, but your children still run and play.
Ask the scribe for more
The scribe writes down one more child under your name and says nothing.
The scribe says the numbers on the tablet cannot be changed.
The copper ship
A big ship is loaded with hundreds of ox-hide copper ingots, tin, blue glass ingots, ivory and oil jars. It will sail west along the Anatolian coast, and the master needs one more hand.

In 1982 a Turkish sponge diver found the wreck at Uluburun, from about 1300 BCE, with nearly 500 copper ingots, tin, glass, ivory, amber and goods from Egypt, Cyprus and Greece. We do not know where it came from or was going, or whether the crew survived.
Sign on
Survived the sinking of a ship carrying ten tons of copper
The wind drives the ship onto an underwater reef and it goes down with everything. You cling to an oil jar and drift ashore, but many of your shipmates are never seen again.
The voyage goes well, and your share is one blue glass ingot.
Stay ashore
That year there is news of a big ship that never came home. You never learn whether it was that one.
No tin
The ships that used to bring tin no longer come. The scribe lists you among the smiths “without allotment”; this year half the smiths have nothing to work.

The Pylos tablets list hundreds of bronze-smiths and the bronze each was given; some are marked a-ta-ra-si-jo, “without allotment”. Tin came from very far away, perhaps as far as Central Asia. When trade faltered, the smiths had nothing to work.
Melt down old bronze
You buy broken knives and old bronze pots from every house and melt them into spearheads for the palace.
Try working iron like the strangers do
Worked iron for the first time
Iron is harder than you thought and needs a fierce fire, but the ore can be found in the hills nearby.
Wait for the tin ships
The ships do not come.
A matter of life or death
A letter arrives from the Hittite king ordering Ugarit to send a great ship of grain, for his land is starving: “It is a matter of life or death!”

Clay letters from Ugarit show that decades before the collapse the Hittite kingdom was short of food and asked Egypt and Ugarit for grain. One letter from the Hittite king calls a grain shipment “a matter of life or death”.
Help load the grain
The city’s granaries run low, but the ship sails as ordered.
Hide your family’s grain
You bury a jar of grain under the floor, against worse days.
The coast-watchers
The palace orders men to watch the coast day and night, and calls up thirty rowers to go to Pleuron. No one says what they are afraid of.

Tablets from Pylos’s last year record rowers sent to Pleuron and lists of men usually read as “thus the watchers are guarding the coast”. Many scholars think the palace knew danger was coming, but not from whom.
Go and watch the coast
You stare at the sea every night until you see ships’ lights even in your dreams.
Take your family up into the hills
You leave the house behind. The neighbours call you a coward.
Strangers from the sea
Several boats run up on the beach, with men, women, children and ox-carts. They speak a tongue no one understands, are thin as sticks, and say with their hands that their homes were burned.

Egyptian carvings show some “Sea Peoples” travelling with families and ox-carts, not only warriors. Many were probably refugees from drought and war. People called invaders in one place may have been fleeing from another.
Let them settle at the edge of the village
A year later they teach you a new way to make pots, and your children pick up words of their tongue.
Drive them away
The boats sail on down the coast. You wonder what the next village will do.
Trade grain for their tools
You get an iron knife, sharper than any you have owned.
The ruined palace
Your grandchildren play hide-and-seek in the burned palace and ask who could have built walls of such huge stones.

Later Greeks saw the gigantic walls of Mycenae and Tiryns and believed the Cyclopes had built them; archaeologists still call such walls “Cyclopean” ✦. Tales of a war at Troy were sung on until they became Homer’s epics centuries later.
Tell them ordinary people like their grandparents built it
They do not believe you; ordinary people could never lift such stones, they say.
Tell them of heroes and giants
They listen until dark and tell it to their friends the next day. The story grows every time.
Signs no one uses
There is no palace left to keep accounts for. A grandchild asks what the scratches on the old clay tablet in the house are.
After the palaces fell, Linear B disappeared from Greece, which had no writing for some 400 years. Writing in this age was tied to palace accounts; when the palaces went, so did writing.
Teach the signs you remember
The child learns three or four and forgets them, for there is nothing to write.
Sing the old stories instead
A song lasts longer than a tablet.
A letter to the king of Alashiya

King Ammurapi calls you in the middle of the night to write a letter to the king of Cyprus. He speaks slowly: “My father, behold, the enemy’s ships came; my cities were burned … my troops and chariots are in the Hittite land, and all my ships are in the land of Lukka, so the country is abandoned to itself.”

The letter of Ammurapi, the last king of Ugarit, was found in the city’s ruins, one of the last voices of a Bronze Age world falling apart. We do not know whether it was ever sent. Soon afterwards the city was destroyed. You are a scribe the game made up, but the words come from the real tablet.
Write every word as the king speaks
Wrote one of the last letters of Ugarit
The clay is not yet dry when someone outside shouts that there is fire at the harbour.
Write it, then flee with your family at once
You leave the tablet on the table and lead your family into the hills before dawn. You never go back.
Rose-scented oil
The palace orders dozens of jars of perfumed oil, scented with rose and with sage, to send across the sea as gifts and to offer to the gods.

Pylos tablets record olive oil scented with rose and with sage, and the oil-boilers who made it for the palace. Perfumed oil was an important export, shipped in stirrup jars found all over the eastern Mediterranean.
Boil it slowly by the old recipe
The smell of roses fills the palace; even the guards stop to sniff.
Mix in cheap oil to make more
The scribe weighs the jars and writes your oil down as short.
No one notices, and you earn a little extra.
Purple from shellfish
The fishermen bring heaps of sea snails. You must crack the shells for a tiny gland and ferment it into purple dye. The stench makes the whole village complain.

Heaps of crushed murex shells on Crete suggest the Minoans were making purple dye from shellfish by about 1800 BCE. It took thousands of snails to dye one cloth, so purple became the colour of power for thousands of years.
Keep at it despite the smell
The first cloth comes out deep purple, worth ten times a plain one.
Dye with saffron instead
The golden cloth is just as lovely, and no one complains.
The chariot wheels
A scribe counts the chariot wheels in the store. Many pairs are useless. Your commander says that if war comes, half the chariots will never leave the gates.

Tablets from Knossos and Pylos count chariots, wheels and armour in detail, including wheels marked “unserviceable”. Chariots were costly elite weapons across the Near East. Some argue that new foot soldiers with javelins and long swords made chariots less decisive late in the age, but this is debated.
Mend the wheels yourself
You work until your hands blister and bring five more chariots back into service.
Train to fight on foot instead
Your friends laugh to see you practising the javelin like a commoner.
In winter the whole family beats the olive branches so the fruit drops onto cloths spread below, and the children chase the ones that roll away.
Olives gave food, lamp oil, medicine and perfume. The great jars taller than a man, called pithoi, in the storerooms of Knossos held vast amounts of oil, grain and wine.
A pod of dolphins leaps beside your father’s boat. You count twelve before they vanish.
Dolphins and fish were favourite Minoan designs on pots and walls. The famous dolphin painting at Knossos was largely restored in Evans’s time from only a few fragments.
You catch an octopus in a rock pool. It squirts ink until you are black from head to toe.
Octopuses with tentacles spreading all around the jar are a hallmark of the Minoan pottery called “Marine Style”.
An earthquake in the night. Pots crash down all over the house and everyone runs out to sleep in the yard until morning.

Crete and Greece lie on active faults, and earthquakes are common. Several Minoan palaces were rebuilt after great quakes. Today most scholars do not think earthquakes alone brought down the Bronze Age.
All day carts haul oil jars down to the harbour, jars with little handles shaped like stirrups.
A wild billy goat with long curved horns stands still on the cliff, looking down at your goats.
The Cretan wild goat, or kri-kri, still lives in Crete’s mountains today as a protected animal, and appears on many Minoan seals.
A seal basks on the rocks outside a sea cave. The fishermen say it steals fish from their nets.
The Mediterranean monk seal was once found all over this sea. Today it is one of the rarest seals in the world, with only a few hundred left, mostly in Greece and Turkey.
The whole village climbs the mountain at night, lights a great fire, and throws little clay figures of people, cattle and arms and legs into it.

Thousands of little clay figures of people, animals and body parts have been found on Cretan mountain tops, which archaeologists call peak sanctuaries. The body parts may have been prayers for healing, but we do not know whom the Minoans worshipped, because we cannot read their writing.
In a sacred underground store stands a figure of a woman holding up a snake in each hand, wearing a skirt of many flounces.

Faience figures of women holding snakes were found at Knossos, from about 1600 BCE. Scholars call them “snake goddesses” but do not know whether they show goddesses or priestesses. Tellingly, some similar figures in foreign museums have turned out to be 20th-century forgeries.
At the door of the shrine a double axe is carved into the pillar, and stone horns stand in a row along the roof.
The double axe (labrys) and the “horns of consecration” are common symbols in Minoan holy places. Both are probably linked to bulls and sacrifice, but their real meaning is interpretation.
Workers are building a great tomb for the royal family. Inside is a stone dome as tall as a four-storey house, reached by a long passage cut into the hill.

The domed tomb later Greeks called the “Treasury of Atreus” was built around 1250 BCE. Its dome, about 13 metres high, was the largest in the world for over a thousand years. The name comes from legend ✦; we do not know who was buried there.
A scribe recites letters in a row, one sound at a time, thirty in all, and the pupils press wedges into clay for each sound they hear.

Ugarit used a new cuneiform alphabet of only 30 letters, around 1400 BCE. Tablets listing the letters in order have been found, and the order is similar to the one later used in many alphabets. A system of a few dozen signs was far easier for ordinary people to learn than cuneiform with its hundreds.
At a palace feast a musician plays the lyre and sings to the goddess Nikkal from a clay tablet with both words and numbers showing how to play.

A clay tablet from Ugarit, about 1400 BCE, records a Hurrian hymn with instructions for the lyre: the oldest substantially complete melody known. But it can be transcribed in several ways, so any version we hear today is a guess.
Smoke from the copper furnaces rises from the hills day and night. The forest round the mines has been cut bare for charcoal.
In the market Egyptian, Hittite, Cypriot and Greek traders haggle in their own tongues while interpreters run back and forth.
News comes with a boat that another great city has burned. No one knows who did it: some say pirates, some say starving people rose up.
Strangers come ashore in the night, take sheep from the pen and vanish out to sea.
The village has moved up onto a hill with a long view of the sea, in case strange ships come.
A new smith in the village makes knives from ore dug in the hills. No one has to wait for ships from far away any more.
Your eyes are so dim that a grandchild must thread the loom for you.
You sit on the stone outside the house in the evening and watch the boats come in, as you did as a child.
Waves lap softly on the shore rocks.
Sheep bleat on the hillside.
Cicadas shrill all through the olive grove.
A sailing ship passes far out.
The sea wind blows the smell of salt into the house.
Women grind barley outside the houses.
Gulls cry over the harbour.
Hearth smoke rises in the evening.
Goats clamber over the rocks for leaves.
A few generations after you, most Minoan palaces will burn. Mycenaeans from the mainland will rule Knossos and keep accounts in Greek, and the language of your grandparents will slowly fade away.

Within a few generations the palaces, ports and kingdoms around the sea will fall one after another: Pylos, Mycenae, Ugarit and the Hittite capital Hattusa. The world you knew will vanish in less than a lifetime.
You lived as the old world fell apart. Your descendants will live in small villages with no palaces, no writing, and trade only with their neighbours.
In about three hundred years your descendants will borrow letters from the Phoenicians, build a new kind of city called the polis, and sing of the heroes of the palace age your grandparents knew.

Then these palaces were left only as legends: King Minos, the Minotaur, the Trojan War ✦. Until Schliemann dug Mycenae in 1876, Evans dug Knossos in 1900, a farmer’s plough found Ugarit in 1928, and Ventris read Linear B in 1952. The Minoans’ Linear A still cannot be read today.
The seals you saw number only a few hundred in the Mediterranean today.
The Cretan wild goat still lives in Crete’s mountains, under protection.

The Bronze Age did not fall for one reason. Every palace depended on the others across the sea: copper from Cyprus, tin from far away, grain from Egypt. When drought, earthquakes, migrations, pirates and revolts came together, the tightly linked system came apart piece by piece. The richest palaces fell first, because they relied most on distant trade, while villages that fed themselves survived. Scholars still argue which cause mattered most, but the lesson is that the more connected a world is, the richer and the more fragile it becomes.
You wrote some {0} clay tablets. The fire that burned the city baked them hard; in this game {1} survive underground, perhaps among those archaeologists read today.
You wrote some {0} clay tablets, but no fire ever baked them, and rain and damp turned them back into mud.
King Ammurapi’s letter really survives today. In this game, the hand that wrote it was yours.
You yourself were one of those who adapted as the world changed.

Minoans often buried their dead together in family or village tombs used for centuries, sometimes in painted clay coffins. Mycenaeans buried families in chambers cut into hillsides, and great people in domed tombs. Broken drinking cups are often found at tomb doors, perhaps from a farewell toast. After the palaces fell, some places began to cremate the dead and put the ashes in jars.
Drink a farewell and break the cup at the tomb door
The crack of the cup echoes down the tomb passage, and everyone falls silent.
Lay the things they loved beside them
You lay a comb, a clay lamp and an octopus-painted jar beside the body.
Burn the body and keep the ashes in a jar
The smoke rises high. You gather the ashes into a jar and bury it near the new house.
Your family burns your body and buries the ashes in a clay jar near the hilltop village.
min
You are buried in the family tomb with a gold ring and stone cups.
You are laid in the family’s domed tomb with a bronze sword, a gold cup and an ivory comb.
You are buried in a small pit outside the tomb of the family you served, with a single pot.
You are laid in a clay coffin painted with octopuses, in the village’s shared tomb.
You are laid in the family chamber cut into the hillside, beside your grandparents.
Those who reach 50 by the Aegean have seen countless ships from far lands. If one day the ships stopped coming, how would they live?
The cities around the sea have fallen one by one. No ships, no tin, no letters. If you had to teach your grandchildren to survive in a world where no one helps anyone, what would you teach them?
raiders from the sea
The winter rains never come. The wells dry up and the barley dies before it heads.
A great earthquake. Stone walls collapse and many roofs fall in.
Your tablet, baked hard by the fire. The game’s marks imitate the look of palace accounts; they are not real signs.
An unbaked tablet: most like it melted back into mud. The game’s marks are not real signs.
The rice of your Yangtze lands will one day feed billions. Farmers from here will move south, carrying rice and pigs into Southeast Asia, including today’s Thailand, about 4,000 years ago.

The millet of your Yellow River lands, with rice from the Yangtze, will one day feed billions. Farmers from here will move south, carrying rice and pigs into Southeast Asia, including today’s Thailand, about 4,000 years ago.
It grows up and barks whenever anything nears the camp.

Over the next tens of thousands of years your species will spread across the world and become the only human species left. All 8 billion people alive today descend from Africans of your time, though the earliest groups to leave Africa may have left no descendants today; this is still debated.

Thousands or tens of thousands of years after your time, the ice melts, the sea swallows the Beringia land bridge, and mammoths vanish from the mainland. People will start planting seeds. The last mammoths, on Wrangel Island, survive until about 4,000 years ago, after Egypt’s pyramids were already built.

In the centuries after you, in some places up to two thousand years later, the descendants of voyagers like you settled the whole Polynesian Triangle, from Hawaiʻi and Rapa Nui to Aotearoa, across an ocean wider than any continent, by canoe and star knowledge, without maps or compass. In 1976 the canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti by traditional wayfinding and proved it could be done.
the Old Babylonian period

Mesopotamian society was layered. Law codes from Ur-Nammu’s (about 2100 BCE) to Hammurabi’s (about 1754 BCE) distinguish free citizens, commoners and slaves, and the same offence carried different penalties. Many people worked for a temple or palace in return for rations. Some slaves were war captives; others fell into slavery through debt.

Cuneiform went on being written for about two thousand more years; the last known tablet is an astronomical text from about 75 CE. After that no one could read it until scholars deciphered it in the 1850s. Hundreds of thousands of tablets have been excavated, and many have never been read.
Thebes, the southern town that later became the city of Amun

Thebes (Waset) was a small town in early times and became the city of Amun from the Middle Kingdom, with the temple of Karnak, added to for nearly two thousand years. Across the river lay the city of the dead, including the Valley of the Kings in the New Kingdom.
“Neith is satisfied”
The pyramids of your age will stand for more than 4,500 years. Of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, only the Great Pyramid still stands.
the one who still remembers the marks for counting sheep
the family of a local chief (basileus)
landless people who work other people’s fields
slaves in another family’s house
After the palaces fell, there were no palace rations and no scribes. Power passed to local chiefs: the word basileus, once a minor palace title in Linear B (qa-si-re-u), later came to mean king.

Studies combining data from many pre-modern societies found that about 1 in 4 children died before their first birthday, and nearly half before reaching their teens. In Thailand today, fewer than 1 in 100 children die before age five. Think about what changed to make that difference.
What is the first sound a five-year-old hears each morning in a mud-brick city?
What might a five-year-old by the Nile fear most, and love most?
If this child drew a picture in the dust, what would it be?
A five-year-old by the sea watches a strange ship come in. Where does the child think it came from?
Classroom
still children:
· The family’s herd:
Your family buries your small body in a clay urn near the house, not in the lineage cemetery like the grown-ups.
One of your children falls ill and dies. The family buries the little body near the house in a clay urn.
the early Shang, when the capital was still at Zhengzhou
the move of the capital to Yin, and the reign of King Wu Ding
the late Shang
the early Zhou, after the fall of the Shang
the Shang city at Zhengzhou, inside its walls of pounded earth
Panlongcheng, the Shang outpost on the Yangtze
Yin, the Shang capital on the Huan River
Sanxingdui, a kingdom’s city in the Sichuan basin
the plain of Zhou, below Mount Qi in the west
a farming village on the Central Plain
rice, millet and beans
millet, wheat and beans

The Shang city at Zhengzhou was built around 1600–1500 BCE. Its pounded-earth walls run for nearly 7 kilometres; tens of thousands of people beat the earth in layer after layer. Bronze foundries and bone workshops lie outside the walls. Whether this was the capital that later books call Bo or Ao is still debated.

Panlongcheng, near today’s Wuhan, is a walled town built just like the Shang cities of the north, about 450 kilometres away. It probably helped send copper and tin from the south up to the northern bronze foundries.

Yin, near today’s Anyang, was the last Shang capital, from about 1300 BCE until the fall in 1046 BCE. It had palace and temple halls on pounded-earth platforms, a royal cemetery across the river, and foundries and workshops for bronze, bone and pottery. Almost all the oracle bones we have come from here.

Sanxingdui, in Sichuan, was a different civilisation, not Shang. Its smiths cast bronze masks with bulging eyes, a standing figure 2.6 metres tall and a bronze tree nearly 4 metres high, like nothing else in the world. They knew the Shang and owned Shang-style vessels, yet not a single written sign has been found there.

The plain of Zhou, below Mount Qi in the Wei valley, was home to the Zhou, who would one day overthrow the Shang. The Zhou also divined with turtle shells; in 1977 more than 17,000 pieces of Zhou shell and bone were found here, some carved with signs so small you need a magnifying glass to read them.

Most people in the Shang age did not live in palaces but in villages, in houses dug half into the ground with thatched roofs. They grew millet, kept pigs and dogs, and owed grain and labour to their lords. The oracle bones call farmers zhong, “the multitude”, whom the king sent to till fields or to fight.

In the oracle bones a person’s name is often a single sign. Shang kings were called by the day of the ten-day week on which their descendants made offerings to them: Wu Ding is a “ding” day. Women of the court are called Fu, “lady”. Ordinary people’s names hardly survive, so the names in the game are invented.
a child who scares birds from the millet
a farmer whose granary is never empty
the elder the whole village heeds
Cattle-keeper
a child who minds the pigs
a cattle-keeper
a keeper of the cattle for the rites
keeper of the king’s herds
Diviner
Prepare shells, crack them with fire and carve the king’s questions
a child who scrapes turtle shells
a bone engraver
a diviner of the court
the diviner whose name is carved on a thousand shells
Bone and jade carver
Saw cattle bone into hairpins and arrowheads
a child who polishes bone pins
a bone carver
a carver of jade animals
master of the bone workshop
Bronze caster
Make clay moulds and cast bronze vessels
a bronze caster
a carver of beast-face patterns in the moulds
master of the royal foundry
Shape three-legged pots and grain jars
an apprentice who kneads clay
a potter of pale green glazed jars
the potter whose jars are used in the palace rites

a child who picks mulberry leaves
a silk-worker
a weaver of patterned silk
head of the palace silk rooms
Train with the dagger-axe and the bow
a boy who carries the shields
leader of the lineage’s warriors
the best archer in the company

Yin had separate workshop districts: great bronze foundries, bone workshops that used tons of cattle bone, potteries and jade workshops. Later records say crafts passed down within lineages, and that after the fall the Zhou handed out whole Shang craft lineages to their new lords.
a noble lineage close to the king
a farming family, one of the zhong, “the multitude”
a craft family working for the king’s workshops
a war captive serving a noble household

Shang society was organised by lineage. The king and nobles made offerings to their ancestors; farmers tilled and went to war when called. Captives from enemies such as the Qiang were made to work, and many were killed in sacrifices: the oracle bones record more than 13,000 people offered.
a Shang noble lineage that must now serve the Zhou
a craft family handed over to a Zhou lord
bone hairpins
silk cloth
The rains do not come in season, and the millet yellows before it heads.
The rains come just right, and the millet heads hang so heavy they touch the ground.

The most common questions on the oracle bones are about rain and harvest, such as “Will we receive millet harvest?” The Shang kings believed a high god called Di commanded wind and rain, and that the ancestors could ask on their behalf.
There is no Shang king left to divine for, but the Zhou lords need people who can write. Now you carve their names into the moulds for bronze vessels instead.

The Zhou took over the Shang script entirely and employed many Shang scribes. Unlike Greece after the Bronze Age collapse, where writing vanished altogether, Chinese writing carried on without a break to this day.
Carved your first oracle bone
Every family must send hands to the walls. Earth is poured into wooden frames one layer at a time and beaten with poles until it is as hard as stone.

Pounded earth, hangtu, was how Chinese walls and platforms were built for thousands of years. Stretches of the Shang wall at Zhengzhou still stand today, and some later sections of the Great Wall were built the same way.
News comes that the king has moved the capital north, to Yin on the Huan River. Some of the nobles grumble that they do not want to go.

Later books say King Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin around 1300 BCE and had to talk round nobles who did not want to move. The Shang moved their capital many times, but after this they stayed at Yin until the end.
The first chariot you have ever seen rattles down the street, two horses pulling wheels with dozens of spokes. It is so loud the children scatter.
Horse-drawn chariots reached China around 1200 BCE, probably from the steppes to the north-west. At Yin, chariots were buried with their pairs of horses, sometimes with a driver as well.
King Wu Ding is dead and the whole city mourns. The procession crosses the river to the royal cemetery, where the burial pit is deeper than three houses stacked up.

The Shang royal tombs at Xibeigang are cross-shaped pits about 10 metres deep with four ramps leading down. Robbers emptied almost all of them before archaeologists arrived. Around them lie more than a thousand pits holding sacrificed people and animals.
The king marches east against the Renfang for most of a year. Many of the village men are not home for the harvest.
Late oracle bones record a long campaign against the Renfang, the “Eastern Yi”. Some historians think the wars in the east left the Shang weak just when the Zhou came from the west.

The army of Zhou and its allies breaks the Shang host on the plain of Muye. Word goes round that the king climbed a tall tower, dressed himself in jade and set it on fire. Zhou soldiers walk into the city and no one stops them.
People fleeing the capital say the Shang king has lost. A new house called Zhou, from the west, will rule now.
The Zhou won at Muye around 1046 BCE (the year is still debated). The story of the last king burning himself comes from records written centuries later ✦.
Lived through the fall of the Shang
The last king’s son rises against the Zhou, and is crushed within three years. The Zhou order many Shang lineages to move to a new city in the west.

Zhou texts say Wu Geng, son of the last Shang king, rebelled together with some Zhou princes. The Duke of Zhou put it down and moved Shang families to the new city of Luoyi (today’s Luoyang). The Shang royal line was given the small state of Song so it could keep making offerings to its ancestors.
The leaders order the bronze masks smashed and the bronze trees burned, then buried in pits with hundreds of elephant tusks. No one tells you why.

The Sanxingdui pits were found in 1986 and in 2019–2022. Radiocarbon dates put the burials in the late Shang, about 3,200–3,000 years ago. Everything in them was broken and burned before burial, but no one knows why, because the people of Sanxingdui left no writing at all.
You help carry cattle bones to the workshop and are paid in millet.

The Shang had no coins. Wealth meant grain, silk, bronze and cowrie shells from the southern seas. Kings gave cowries as rewards, and many Chinese characters to do with wealth, such as 貝, still contain the picture of a cowrie today.
a child of a noble lineage

Carve questions and answers into turtle shells

Feed the piglets

Catch shrimp and snails at the bank

Listen to grandmother’s tale of the ten suns
Watch the sky and count the days of the sixty-day cycle
The crack of the shell
You peek as a diviner presses a glowing stick into a little hollow on the back of a turtle shell. There is a sharp “pok”, and a crack shaped like 卜 appears.

Workers drilled and chiselled rows of small hollows into the back of a shell or an ox shoulder blade. When heated, the front cracked in a 卜 shape. The character 卜, “to divine”, comes from this crack, and its sound is thought to echo the crack itself.
Ask what the crack says
The diviner says the ancestors have answered, but only the king can read the answer.
Take a scrap of shell and try to crack it yourself
You burn your fingers, and your mother smacks you for meddling with sacred things.
It cracks in a crooked line. You tell your friends it means rain tomorrow.
The king’s elephant
The king’s hunters lead an elephant through the village. It is taller than the roofs, and the children run after it until the grown-ups drag them back.

In the Shang age northern China was warmer than today and had elephants and rhinoceroses. Oracle bones ask “Will we capture elephants?”, an elephant skeleton was found at Yin, and several Shang bronze vessels are shaped like elephants.
Go up and touch its trunk
It flicks its trunk and knocks you flat on your bottom.
The trunk is warm and rough as bark.
Draw it in the dirt
You draw a long trunk, a round body and four legs. It looks a lot like the sign 象 the diviners use.
The silkworms
In a dark room hundreds of silkworms munch mulberry leaves with a sound like rain. Grandmother sets you to gathering the white cocoons into a basket.
Traces of silk cling to Shang bronzes and weapons, and the oracle bones have signs for silkworm, silk and mulberry. Evidence of silk in China goes back thousands of years before that.
Gather them carefully
Grandmother says your hands are as gentle as a grown-up’s.
Keep one worm secretly
It spins a cocoon and turns into a white moth that cannot fly.
The mask with bulging eyes
At a festival the grown-ups raise a bronze mask bigger than you are. Its eyes stick out like horns and its ears spread like wings.

The largest Sanxingdui bronze mask is almost 1.4 metres wide, with eyes jutting out about 16 centimetres. Some think it shows an ancestor who sees far ✦; much later books tell of a first king of Shu with “protruding eyes” ✦.
Stare into its eyes without blinking
You always blink first, but you will try again next year.
Ask who made it
Your father points at a smith whose hands are covered in burn scars.
The engraver’s apprentice
A bone engraver needs an apprentice. He says you must learn thousands of signs and practise cutting tiny letters into hard shell with a bronze knife without your hand shaking.
One bone carries the sixty-day calendar carved over and over, some rows neat and some crooked. Scholars think it is an apprentice’s practice piece, with the teacher’s rows as the model.
Become the apprentice
By the end of the first year you can carve all sixty day-names, even if some are crooked.
The elders of two lineages meet to talk of marrying you to someone from a lineage in the next village. But before anything is agreed, the ancestors must be asked.
The Shang married between lineages and believed important decisions needed the ancestors’ approval first. The king divined even about his consorts’ childbirths.
The crack on the ox shoulder blade says good. The wedding has roast pork and drum songs.
Both lineages grumble, but agree to wait.
The king’s hunt
The king is going hunting, and the village must send beaters to drive the animals towards his archers. Word is that this year they will hunt rhinoceros.

Shang kings hunted constantly, and asked the ancestors before every hunt. One bone records a hunt that took hundreds of deer. The late Shang bronze rhinoceros of Xiaochen Yu bears an inscription about a reward the king gave after returning from a campaign.
Go as a beater
A rhinoceros charges back through the line of beaters, and you do not jump clear in time.
You see a living rhinoceros for the first time. Its hide is thick as armour.
Find a way to stay with the fields
The village headman gives you a sour look.
The village bone-reader
One of your children has a fever that will not break. Relatives say to take a pig to the village bone-reader, who will crack a shoulder blade to learn which ancestor is angry.

Divination was not only for the palace. Burned ox and sheep shoulder blades without any writing turn up at many ordinary village sites. Villagers asked their ancestors too, but did not write the questions down.
Take the pig to the bone-reader
The crack says your great-grandfather is hungry. You make him an offering, and a few days later the fever breaks.
Boil herbs for the child yourself
You sit up all night. By morning the fever is slowly falling.
Fu Hao’s army

A runner arrives in the village: the king has sent his consort Fu Hao to lead an army against the Qiang. Her own lineage sends three thousand men, and ten thousand more must be raised from the villages.

One oracle bone records raising “three thousand of Fu Hao’s men and ten thousand troops” to attack the Qiang. Fu Hao was a consort of King Wu Ding who led armies many times and performed rites herself. She is one of the earliest women anywhere known to have led armies.
March with the army
A Qiang arrow strikes your shoulder. You come home with a scar and a story for the rest of your life.
Marched in Fu Hao’s army
You see Fu Hao standing in her chariot with a great bronze axe. The army comes home with captives and cattle.
Hide in the woods until the army has gone
No one comes looking for you, but the whole village knows.
Sending the shells
Your lord orders the village to send two hundred and fifty turtle shells to the king before winter. You spend a month wading in the marshes after turtles.

Many shells carry a short note on the edge saying who sent how many to the palace, such as “Que sent in 250”. Some shells came from far to the south, showing how wide the network sending goods to the king was.
Catch turtles until you have enough
Your legs are raw from the marsh water, but the village’s name is carved on the edge of a shell.
Trade a pig to a merchant for shells
The merchant grins. He got those shells from the south for half the price.
The captive who works beside you
A Qiang man, captured and put to work beside you for two years, has taught you songs from his home. Today soldiers come to take him with the other captives for the rites to the ancestors.
Say nothing
For years you sing his song to yourself, never knowing what the words mean.
Beg your master to keep him for work
Your master says good workers are hard to find and sends someone else instead. You do not know whether to feel glad.
Your master shouts at you to get back to work.
The day of the rites
Every time there are great rites, soldiers come to choose captives from the noble houses. The day of the rites is near again.
Work so hard your master cannot do without you
Your master tells the soldiers you are the household’s craftsman. They choose someone else.
Run for the hills at night
Escaped captivity
You walk for many nights until you reach a distant village where no one asks where you came from.
The guards’ dogs catch your scent before you reach the river. You are dragged back and beaten.
The march east
The king will march against the Renfang in the east again. Last time ten men went from the village and six came home.
The long late-Shang campaigns against the Renfang lasted months and needed great numbers of men and supplies. The bronze rhinoceros of Xiaochen Yu mentions this campaign in its inscription.
Go with the army
You come home with a limp you will keep for life.
The army returns with captives and cowries, and you get a small share.
Ask a kinsman to go in your place
Your kinsman goes, and comes back so thin you hardly know him.
The plain of Muye
King Wu of Zhou calls every lineage to march east. The armies of many allied peoples will gather where the Yellow River is crossed.
The army from the west has crossed the Yellow River. The Shang king is calling up everyone who can hold a spear, captives included.

Zhou-era texts say King Wu swore an oath at Muye before the battle, and that the Shang front ranks turned their weapons on their own side ✦. This was written by the winners, so historians read it with care.
Go to the battle
The battle lasts a single day; your wound takes a year to heal.
Stood on the field of Muye
By morning the Shang host has broken, and you march into Yin with King Wu’s army.
Before noon the front ranks scatter. You drop your spear and run for home.
Take your family out of the armies’ path
You hear the war drums from a distant hill, and do not learn who won for days.
The move to the new city
A Zhou official reads out the order: your lineage must move to the new city of Luoyi, work for the new dynasty, and never think of rebellion again.

The Book of Documents holds Zhou proclamations to the Shang people who were moved, saying Heaven had taken the right to rule from the Shang because their last king did wrong, and promising land and homes to those who obeyed. This is the idea of the Mandate of Heaven, used to explain every change of dynasty in China for three thousand years.
Go with your lineage
Was moved to the new Zhou city
At Luoyi you get a small pounded-earth house, and neighbours who speak with a Shang accent like yours.
Slip away to your mother’s kin in the villages
No one follows. The farmers do not care who is king, so long as it rains.
The leftover piece
While the bronzes are being smashed into the pit, a small piece of mask flies off and lands by your foot. No one sees.
More than ten thousand objects have come out of the Sanxingdui pits — bronze, gold, jade and ivory — but no royal tombs, no clear palace and no writing, so this civilisation remains a mystery.
Throw it into the pit with the rest
It vanishes under the earth and ash, like everything you ever saw at the festivals.
Keep it under your pillow
Every night you rub its edge and think of the bulging eyes that stared at you as a child.
An ancestor who must be fed
A grandchild asks where you will go when you die. You say you will become an ancestor: your descendants must offer you grain and ale on your day, or you will go hungry.

The Shang believed ancestors lived on with real power and, if not fed, could bring sickness or failed harvests. Oracle bones even ask which ancestor caused the king’s toothache. Honouring ancestors is still central to many Chinese families today.
Teach the grandchild every ancestor’s day
The child recites three generations, then asks what day you will be.
Tell the child there is nothing to fear
The child hugs you tight and promises never to forget your offerings.
The winners’ story
Zhou heralds go from village to village saying the last Shang king was cruel and drunk day and night, so Heaven gave the right to rule to the Zhou. Your grandchild turns and asks if it is true.

The picture of the last Shang king with a lake of wine and a forest of meat ✦ comes from texts written centuries later. The oracle bones of his reign show a king still keeping the ancestral rites on schedule and campaigning in the east. Historians must always ask who is telling the story.
Tell what you saw yourself

You tell them the king still kept the rites every ten days and most of the army was away fighting in the east. The child listens wide-eyed, then recites the Zhou story at a friend’s house the next day.
Say the winners are always right
The child nods, and something sticks in your throat.
Fu Hao’s childbirth

On a jiashen day the diviner Que asks the ancestors: “Lady Hao will give birth. Will it be good?” The king reads the cracks: “If she gives birth on a ding day, it will be good; on a geng day, very lucky.” Thirty-one days later Fu Hao gives birth to a daughter. Everyone waits for you to carve the outcome on the shell.

This shell really exists, and records the outcome: “Thirty-one days later, on the jiayin day, she gave birth. It was not good: a girl.” The Shang valued sons more for carrying on the ancestral rites. It is one of the oldest personal records in China.
Carve exactly what happened
Carved the record of Fu Hao’s childbirth
You carve “not good: a girl”, and think of the tiny baby who does not know what has been written about her.
Carve only “She has given birth; mother and child are safe”
The chief diviner scrapes your signs away and carves it again the usual way.
No one notices. But the shell that survives today is not yours.
The moon is eaten
In the middle of the night the moon slowly vanishes into a dark red. The king orders a divination on whether it is a bad omen, and tells you to record the day.

Oracle bones of Wu Ding’s reign record several lunar eclipses with their day in the sixty-day cycle. Modern astronomers can calculate back to when each happened, which helps pin down the years of Wu Ding’s reign.
Record the day as exactly as you can
You carve the day-name with care. Three thousand years later astronomers will use it to work out the year.
Beat drums to drive off whatever is eating the moon
The moon slowly returns, and everyone believes the drums saved it.
The greatest cauldron

The king orders a four-legged bronze cauldron bigger than a cart, for offerings to his mother. Molten bronze must be poured at once from dozens of furnaces; if the pour is not together, it will crack.

The Houmuwu (or Simuwu) ding from Yin weighs about 830 kilograms, the heaviest ancient bronze vessel yet found anywhere. Shang casters used moulds of many fitted clay pieces, unlike the lost-wax method common elsewhere.
Call the rhythm so every furnace pours at once
Molten bronze splashes your arm, but the cauldron comes out whole.
Helped cast the king’s great cauldron
When the moulds are broken away, every line of the beast-face pattern is sharp.
Ask for another month to rehearse
The foundry master is annoyed, but the real pour goes smoothly.
The bone heap
Carts tip cattle bones from the rites in front of the workshop, piled higher than your head. You must choose between plain hairpins and pins carved with birds.
Bone workshops at Yin held tons of cattle bone. Workers turned out hairpins, arrowheads and spoons in great numbers, much like a factory. Bone hairpins were used by Shang people of every rank.
Make plain ones, lots of them
You make dozens a day, until your hands are too calloused to feel the work.
Carve a bird on each
A noble lady sees one and orders twenty.
The chariot
The captain chooses you as the third man on a chariot, standing with the driver and the archer. If it overturns on rough ground, you go down first.

Chariot pits at Yin usually hold one chariot, two horses and sometimes a person. Shang chariots had big wheels with 18–26 spokes, and were probably used as command posts and symbols of power more than for charging the enemy.
Ride the chariot
A wheel hits a rock and you are thrown out with a dislocated shoulder.
Villagers stop to watch the chariot pass, and you try not to grin.
Ask to be a foot archer
Your legs grow stronger every day, and you need not fear the horses.
Signs the size of millet grains
The Zhou diviners carve signs so small you must squint. They say the Shang must never learn what the Zhou ask their ancestors.
Practise carving even smaller
Your eyes ache, but no one can read your signs without taking their time.
Ask what we are asking the ancestors
The diviner answers softly: “We ask whose side Heaven is on.”
At harvest the whole household cuts millet heads with half-moon stone knives and ties them in sheaves to dry outside the house.
Shang farmers still worked mostly with stone and wooden tools. Bronze was too costly for hoes and spades, and went mainly into ritual vessels and the weapons of the elite.
The family dog barks at a stranger all night. Your father says it is the best guard in the village.
Many Shang graves have a small pit beneath the coffin with a dog buried in it, as if to keep guarding its master after death.
The Yellow River runs so thick it looks like flowing mud. The old people say every year it brings new earth to the fields.
The Yellow River carries more silt than almost any river on Earth. It made the Central Plain fertile, but also made the river shift course and flood disastrously again and again in Chinese history.
Every ten days the grown-ups start the count again: jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin, ren, gui. The children chant along like a song.

The Shang counted days in weeks of ten, combined with a set of twelve names into a sixty-day cycle. On the last day of every ten-day week the king asked whether the next ten days would be free of disaster. The sixty cycle is still used in the Chinese calendar today, for example in naming years.
Today is your great-grandfather’s day. The whole lineage sets out bronze vessels of meat and millet ale and calls his name to come and eat.
The Shang fed their ancestors on a fixed schedule, each on the day matching their name. Most of the splendid bronze vessels in museums around the world today were made for these rites.
A rumour comes from the palace: the king has toothache, and the diviners are asking which ancestor is angry.
The oracle bones often ask about the king’s private troubles — toothache, stomach pains, bad dreams, childbirth — because illness might come from a displeased ancestor.
Grandmother says the high god Di lives in the sky and commands wind, rain and thunder. People cannot ask Di directly; they must ask through the ancestors.
In the temple stands a bronze tree taller than two houses. Nine birds perch on its branches, and a dragon slithers down its trunk.
The Sanxingdui bronze tree stands almost 4 metres tall with nine birds. Some compare it to the legend of the Fusang tree where ten suns rest ✦, a legend written down much later.
A goldsmith beats gold into foil and wraps it round a bronze head. It gleams in the firelight as if alive.
A small alligator suns itself on the lakeshore mud. When you come close it gives a low bellow and slides under the water.
Chinese alligators once lived all along the Yangtze, and drums of alligator skin have been found in Neolithic graves. Today only a few hundred remain in the wild.
Boats loaded with lumps of copper come up from the south and wait at the landing before being hauled north to the capital.
Smoke from the bronze foundry rises all day, and the smell of baked clay moulds drifts to your house.
Hundreds of turtle shells lie drying in rows outside the diviners’ rooms, waiting to be drilled.
The Zhou elders complain that the Shang demand more tribute every year, and that the Shang king once imprisoned their leader.
Later books say the last Shang king once imprisoned King Wen of Zhou ✦, before Wen’s son, King Wu, marched to overthrow the Shang. The Zhou had earlier been Shang allies.
Soldiers come for more grain for the army fighting in the east. The village granary is left half empty.
A Zhou lord builds a new house near the village. His people speak with a strange accent, but still write with the same signs as the Shang.
The Zhou heralds say drunkenness brought down the Shang, and anyone drunk at the rites will be severely punished.
The Book of Documents holds a Zhou decree against heavy drinking, blaming it for the fall of the Shang. The many wine vessels in Shang tombs show that drinking was part of the ancestral rites.
Locusts sweep in like a black cloud and eat the millet down to the stalks.
Oracle bones ask about locusts many times, such as “Will the locusts come?”, so it was a danger people feared.
Your eyes are so dim a grandchild must help you sort the millet from the chaff.
You sit outside the house in the evening, listening to drums from distant rites, as you did as a child.
Pigs grunt in the pen.
The wind blows yellow dust into the house.
Cicadas shrill in the mulberry trees.
Somewhere far off, someone strikes a stone chime.
Women pound millet outside the houses.
Children blow egg-shaped clay ocarinas.
Wild ducks fly south in a long line.
Two dogs chase each other round the village.
Light rain patters on the thatch.

After you, the kings will move their capital several more times, until they settle at Yin around 1300 BCE. There diviners will carve questions into more than a hundred thousand shells, the first Chinese writing we can read.

About 150 years after you, the Zhou from the west will overthrow the Shang. But the signs carved by the diviners of your age will not disappear: slowly changing shape, they become the Chinese characters used by more than a billion people today.

Within your descendants’ lifetimes the Zhou will win at Muye, and the Shang, who ruled for about 550 years, will be finished. But Shang people, Shang crafts and Shang writing will live on under the new dynasty.

The Zhou will rule for nearly 800 years, the longest dynasty in Chinese history, and the idea that “Heaven gives the right to rule to the virtuous and takes it back from rulers who do wrong” will be used to explain every change of dynasty for the next three thousand years.

The Sanxingdui civilisation left no writing at all, so we do not know its kings’ names, its language, or why its people buried all their treasures in pits. The region later became the state of Shu, until it was conquered by Qin in 316 BCE.

Then the oracle bones lay underground for more than three thousand years. Farmers dug them up and sold them to apothecaries as “dragon bones”, to be ground into medicine, until in 1899 the scholar Wang Yirong noticed writing on bones he had bought. Archaeologists began digging at Anyang in 1928; in 1936 they found pit YH127 with more than 17,000 pieces of shell, and in 1976 the never-robbed tomb of Fu Hao. Today more than 150,000 pieces are known, with some 4,000–5,000 different signs, about a third of them deciphered.
China’s wild elephants now number about 300, and live only in the far south of Yunnan, more than a thousand kilometres from where you saw yours.
Rhinoceroses have vanished from China altogether.
Only a few hundred Chinese alligators like the one you saw remain in the wild.

Almost everything later Chinese books say about the last Shang king — a lake of wine, a forest of meat, cruel punishments ✦ — was written by the Zhou who overthrew him, or by writers centuries later. The oracle bones let us hear the Shang in their own words: a king worried about rain, toothache, childbirth and his ancestors. Who tells the story shapes the story we hear.
You carved some {0} shells and bones. When they were used up they were buried in storage pits like palace records; in this game {1} survive to today, perhaps in a museum somewhere.
You carved some {0} shells and bones, but none survived. Some may have been ground up as “dragon bones” in an apothecary’s shop.
The shell recording Fu Hao’s childbirth really survives today. In this game, the hand that carved it was yours.
Fu Hao’s tomb was found in 1976, with 468 bronzes, 755 jades and four great bronze axes. You saw her hold an axe like that with your own eyes.
The battle of Muye was one of the turning points of Chinese history, and you stood on the field that day.

The Shang buried their dead in lineage cemeteries, lying on their backs, heads often to the north. Many graves have a little pit under the coffin holding a dog, and cowrie shells were often placed in the mouth. The wealthy took bronze vessels for offerings in the next world; royal tombs had people and animals buried with them.
Bury a dog in the little pit under the coffin
Everyone believes the dog will keep guarding them in the dark.
Place cowrie shells in the mouth
You gently set three cowries in the mouth, in case they are needed in the next world.
Promise offerings on their day, every ten days
You choose their day of the ten-day week. From today they are an ancestor.
Your family buries you in a pit outside the city, with clay pots and jade ornaments.
You are buried in the lineage cemetery with bronze offering vessels, a bronze axe and jade animals, and a dog to guard you under the coffin.
You are buried in a small pit at the edge of the cemetery with nothing, but someone secretly leaves a bone hairpin beside you.
zhou
You are buried in the lineage cemetery in the Shang way, though the Zhou rule now, with clay pots and cowries in your mouth.
You are buried in the lineage cemetery with two clay pots and cowries in your mouth.
A five-year-old in Shang times believes the ancestors answer questions through cracks in turtle shells. If this child could ask one question, what would it be?
The Shang kings asked their ancestors before every hunt, every war and every harvest. If you could ask about only one thing a year, what would you ask?
The Zhou tell everyone that Heaven took power from the Shang because the last king was wicked. You lived through it. Whose story will your grandchildren believe?
war
a noble household’s sacrificial rites
The rains never come. The yellow earth cracks and the millet dies as seedlings.
The river breaks its banks in the night, and yellow mud-water fills the sunken houses to the roofs.
A shell you carved, with its 卜-shaped cracks and questions running down in columns. The game’s signs only imitate the look; they are not real characters.
knows the signs

Your family buries your small body beneath the house floor, so you can stay close to everyone.
One of your children falls ill and dies. The family buries the little body beneath the house floor with a single jade bead.

San Lorenzo stood on a plateau that people built up with fill until it rose above the flood plain. It flourished around 1200–900 BCE. Ten colossal heads have been found here, and long drains made of basalt troughs fitted end to end.

La Venta, on an island in the marshes near the river mouth, flourished around 900–400 BCE. It had a cone-shaped clay mound about 30 metres high, ceremonial plazas, four colossal heads, and pits where tons of serpentine blocks were buried, never to be seen again.
Tres Zapotes lasted longer than the other Olmec towns. Here, in 1862, a farmhand dug up the first colossal head the modern world came to know.

The basalt for the colossal heads came from the Tuxtla mountains, especially the volcano Cerro Cintepec, 60–150 kilometres from the great towns. Boulders weighing tens of tons were moved with no wheels and no animals to pull them.

Chalcatzingo, in the central highlands of Mexico, lies hundreds of kilometres from the coast, yet its cliffs carry Olmec-style carvings, such as a figure seated in a cave mouth from which rain clouds drift. Ideas and precious goods travelled far.

Most people lived in villages of pole houses roofed with palm leaves. They grew maize, beans and squash on riverbank land that flooded every year, caught fish and turtles in the rivers, and raised dogs to eat. Everything was carried on human backs or by canoe.

We do not know what the Olmec called themselves, or the name of a single person. “Olmec” comes from the language of the Aztecs, who lived more than two thousand years later, and means “people of the rubber land”. The names in the game are invented.

The Olmec had no metal tools. Sculptors of the colossal heads pounded with harder stones, polished with wet sand, and drilled details with reeds spun against sand. Jade workers did the same. Their blue-green jade came from the Motagua valley in Guatemala, hundreds of kilometres away.
the family of the ruler and those close to him
a family of farmers and fishers
a craft family working for the ruler

Olmec society had rulers powerful enough to order thousands of people to drag stones weighing tens of tons and heap up great mounds. Elite families probably controlled the best riverbank land, renewed with silt by every flood. Whether anyone was enslaved, we know very little.
jade beads
rubber balls
The seasonal flood covers the riverbank land, then drains away leaving a hand’s depth of fresh mud. The maize will be good this year.
The rains come late and the river never rises over the banks. The first maize wilts.

The Gulf Coast is rainy and floods every year. Riverbank land renewed with fresh silt can grow two maize crops a year. Some archaeologists think Olmec rulers gained their power by controlling these rich lands.
Finished your first colossal head
On the day the last sand is washed from the stone face, the whole town gathers to look. The face you have carved for years looks back at everyone.
Another colossal head you helped carve is finished.
You must work a season for the lender in place of what you still owe.
Every family must carry baskets of earth up to raise the plateau higher still. No oxen, no horses, no carts: only thousands of human backs.

At San Lorenzo people moved enormous amounts of earth in baskets. The Americas had no large animals that could be tamed to pull loads; America’s native horses had died out more than ten thousand years earlier.
People batter the faces of the colossal heads and stone thrones, then drag them to be buried in rows in trenches. A few years later most families have left the town.

Around 900 BCE San Lorenzo declined. Many monuments were damaged and buried. Some think enemies or rebels did it, some that it was a ritual “killing” of monuments when a ruler died, and some that the river changed course and the town lost its importance. No one knows for sure.
Saw San Lorenzo emptied
The cone-shaped clay mound in the middle of town grows higher every year, until from its top you can see the sea.
The rulers are gone. Many monuments are smashed, families drift away from the island, and grass grows over the plazas.
La Venta was abandoned around 400 BCE. Some scholars point to rivers shifting and silting up, making farming and canoe travel around the town harder, but the real causes are still debated.
The volcano’s summit breathes thin smoke all month, and the ground trembles softly at night. The old people say the mountain is breathing.
The Tuxtlas are volcanic mountains. The dense basalt of the colossal heads is cooled lava from these volcanoes.
You help carry bundles of salt and dried fish to an upriver village and are paid in maize.
The Olmec had no money. Valuables were jade, obsidian for blades, iron-ore mirrors, feathers and cacao beans. Everything moved on human backs, for there were no pack animals and no wheels.
a child of the ruling family
