Sappho’s songs
In a house in Mytilene a woman named Sappho teaches girls to sing and play the lyre. She sings of love and longing instead of the war songs the men sing.

Sappho lived about 630–570 BCE. Later Greeks counted her as “the tenth Muse”. Her nine books of poems are almost all lost: only one poem survives complete. Some pieces were found on papyrus used to wrap mummies, and a new poem of hers was identified in 2014.
Ask to learn to sing
Your voice trembles the first time. Sappho smiles and says love makes voices tremble like that.
Listen at the door
You remember only one line, but you sing it until you are old.
The shaking-off of burdens

In the square a man named Solon announces new laws: every debt secured on a person is cancelled, the stone markers that showed land was pledged are pulled up, and Athenians sold as slaves for debt will be bought back.

In 594 BCE Solon was chosen to settle a debt crisis that had brought Athens close to civil war. His reform was called the seisachtheia, “the shaking-off of burdens”. From then on no Athenian could be pledged as security for a debt. Solon wrote poems boasting that he had freed the enslaved earth.
Cheer
Freed by Solon’s law
The poor weep for joy, the rich complain of their losses. Solon says that if both sides are unhappy, he must have got it right.
Ask how long the laws will last
Solon says he will go abroad for ten years, so no one can pester him to change the laws.
The sun goes out
In the afternoon the sky goes dark enough to see stars. The birds fall silent and everyone screams, except an old man named Thales, who stands smiling as if he had been waiting for this.

Herodotus says Thales of Miletus foretold this eclipse ✦, and that the Lydian and Median armies fighting that day were so frightened they made peace. Astronomers date it to 28 May 585 BCE. Scholars doubt how far Thales could really predict it, but he was among the first to explain the world by reasoning rather than gods.
Run and ask Thales
Thales says the Moon has passed in front of the Sun and no god is angry with anyone. You are not sure you believe it, but you are no longer afraid.
Hide under the table
When the light comes back, you hear Thales laughing outside.
The oracle of Delphi
The envoys of King Croesus of Lydia, the richest man in the world, take ship with gold offerings for Delphi, to ask the god whether to make war on Persia. They hire people to help carry.

Herodotus says the god at Delphi answered that if Croesus made war on Persia he would destroy a great empire ✦. Croesus attacked, and the empire destroyed, around 547 BCE, was his own. After that the Greek cities of Ionia came under Persia.
Help carry the gold to Delphi
You hear the oracle with your own ears. The envoys beam, but you wonder which empire it means.
Stay: rumour says Persia is terrible
Two years later the Persian army reaches your coast.
The festival at Olympia
Every four years the Greek cities declare a truce so people can travel safely to Olympia. You go with your family and see a giant wrestler from Croton named Milo, whom no one can throw.

Milo won the wrestling at Olympia six times, the first as a boy, between about 540 and 516 BCE. Legend says he carried a calf every day until it was a bull, so his strength grew day by day too ✦. Olympic athletes competed naked, and married women were barred from watching.
Squeeze to the front
Milo walks past close enough that you smell the olive oil on his skin. His shoulders are as wide as a door.
Go home and carry a kid goat every day
Three months later the goat is too heavy to lift, and you conclude something must be wrong with the legend.
The man who will not eat beans

A man named Pythagoras teaches that everything in the world is number. He plucks a lyre string: a string half as long sounds exactly an octave higher. His followers may not eat broad beans, and nobody knows why.

Pythagoras was born on Samos, near Miletus, and founded a school at Croton in southern Italy around 530 BCE. He wrote nothing himself: the bean rule and the discovery of musical ratios come from later writers ✦. The theorem named after him was known to the Babylonians more than a thousand years earlier.
Measure the strings yourself
Two-thirds of a string sounds a fifth, three-quarters a fourth. You lie awake all night with excitement.
Eat beans in front of him
His followers look at you as if you had eaten your own parents.
The plain of Marathon
The Persian army has landed in the bay of Marathon, about forty kilometres from Athens. Every Athenian with a shield and spear must march, with only a few hundred Plataeans to help.

In 490 BCE the Athenians won at Marathon. Herodotus says 192 Athenians died and about 6,400 Persians. Before the battle a runner named Pheidippides ran about 240 kilometres to Sparta for help in two days. The story of a runner who carried news of victory from Marathon to Athens and then dropped dead is told only centuries later ✦, and gave the marathon race its name.
Charge the Persian line
An arrow strikes your thigh, but you keep running all the way to the enemy ships.
Fought at Marathon
The Persians flee to their ships. For the rest of your life you never tire of telling about this day.
Keep to the back ranks
Was in the army at Marathon
You never stab anyone, but everyone who was at Marathon is called a hero.
The potsherd

On the day of the exile vote, a farmer who cannot read hands you a potsherd and asks you to write “Aristides” on it. You ask what Aristides ever did to him. “Nothing,” he says. “I’m just sick of hearing everyone call him the Just.”
On the day of the exile vote you cannot write, so you hand your potsherd to the man beside you and ask him to write “Aristides”. He asks what Aristides ever did to you.

Athenians used ostracism to send a politician who seemed too powerful out of the city for ten years, writing his name on a broken piece of pottery. At least about 6,000 votes were needed. Plutarch says the man asked to write Aristides’ name was Aristides himself, and that he wrote it ✦. Aristides was ostracised in 482 BCE and recalled before the battle of Salamis. Archaeologists have found thousands of these sherds, some written in the same handwriting.
Write the name as asked
Only later do you learn that the man standing nearby watching was Aristides himself.
Write a different name
That name gets one vote: yours.
The straits of Salamis

Themistocles orders everyone onto the warships. Each trireme needs about 170 rowers, and a poor man who cannot afford a shield is worth as much as a noble once he holds an oar. In the narrow strait the larger Persian fleet crowds and crashes into itself.

In 480 BCE the Greek fleet defeated Persia at Salamis. A trireme had three banks of rowers and a bronze ram on its prow. Afterwards the poor men who rowed gained more say in Athenian politics: many historians think Athenian democracy grew with its navy.
Row until your hands split
Rowed at Salamis
The piper gives the stroke, a hundred oars strike as one, then wood splinters as the ram meets an enemy hull.
Ferry the old and the children to the island
From the island you watch the sea fill with wreckage and smoke, and know who has won only when you see whose ships are fleeing.
The three hundred

King Leonidas picks 300 men to hold the pass of Thermopylae against Persia, choosing only men who already have sons. At a door a mother hands her son his shield and says: “Come back with it, or on it.”

Herodotus writes that Leonidas chose only men with sons. All 300 died in 480 BCE, alongside thousands of other Greeks who are usually forgotten. The Spartan mother’s words, and Leonidas’ answer when the Persians told him to lay down his arms, “Come and take them”, come from Plutarch, writing some six hundred years later ✦.
Watch the men march out
No one weeps, for Spartans may not. You hold it in until your throat aches.
Ask why it must be men with sons
An elder answers shortly: “So that someone carries on the name.”
The play called The Persians

In the open-air theatre below the Acropolis, thousands sit on the hillside to watch Aeschylus’ play about Salamis, told from the side of the weeping Persians. The young man who paid for the chorus is called Pericles.

Aeschylus’ Persians was staged in 472 BCE. It is the oldest Greek play to survive complete, and the only surviving tragedy about real events. Aeschylus himself had fought at Marathon. Its sponsor was Pericles, later leader of Athens.
Weep with the Persians
You are startled to pity the enemy, though your father fought them.
Jeer when the Persian king appears
The whole theatre jeers along. The actor behind the mask stands still.
The storyteller who asks everyone

At Olympia a man from Halicarnassus named Herodotus reads his book aloud to the crowd: the wars with Persia, Egypt where the women go to market and the men weave, and ants as big as dogs that dig up gold. He says he only reports what others told him.

Herodotus called his work historiē, “inquiry”, which became our word history. He is called “the father of history”, and by some “the father of lies” for tales like the gold-digging ants. The story of his reading at Olympia comes from a much later writer ✦.
Ask whether he saw the ants himself
He says no, but many Persians told the same story, and he writes down your question too.
Tell him about your home town
He listens intently. All your life you wonder whether your story ended up in his book.
The funeral speech

In the first winter of the war the whole city goes to the cemetery outside the walls to bury the dead soldiers. Pericles climbs a high platform and says that Athens is the school of all Greece, and that a man who takes no interest in public affairs is not quiet but useless.

This speech comes from Thucydides, who says plainly that he wrote speeches as they “ought to have been” given, since he could not remember them word for word: so it is both Pericles’ thought and Thucydides’. The line that Athens is a democracy because power lies with the many comes from here, yet most of the people listening could not vote.
Listen to the end
The women are told to stay quiet and unspoken of, though they are the ones weeping at the graves.
Look for a name you know on the stone
The names are listed by tribe, without fathers’ names or rank. Everyone is equal in death.
The doctor from Kos

A travelling doctor named Hippocrates comes to see your relative, who falls to the ground in fits. Everyone says the gods are punishing him, but this doctor makes no offering. He feels the pulse, asks what the man eats and where he drinks, and writes everything down.

Hippocrates (about 460–370 BCE) and his pupils wrote more than sixty medical books. One, On the Sacred Disease, says epilepsy is no more sacred than any other illness and has natural causes. The Hippocratic Oath that doctors still speak of may have been written by later members of his school.
Help the doctor take notes
The doctor says, “Life is short, the art is long,” then teaches you to study the colour of urine, which you never wanted to know.
Offer a cockerel to the god as well, just in case
The doctor sees and says nothing, except that your relative should eat the cockerel as soup instead.
The man who never stops asking

In the market a barefoot old man with a snub nose named Socrates stops you and asks, “What is courage?” You answer; he asks again; you answer again, until at last you feel you know nothing at all. The crowd laughs.

Socrates wrote no books at all; we know him from his pupils, above all Plato. His way of asking question after question until we see our beliefs contradict each other is still called the Socratic method. In Plato’s dialogues Socrates says he is wiser than others only in not thinking he knows what he does not.
Question him back
Socrates laughs with delight and asks something even harder. You go home and argue with your mother all night.
Walk away
He calls after you that walking away from a question is a kind of answer too, which is even more annoying.
Five hundred and one jurors

You are chosen by lot as a juror. Today the defendant is Socrates, seventy years old, charged with not honouring the city’s gods and corrupting the young. He begs for no mercy, and says: “The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.”

In 399 BCE a jury of about 500, all male citizens over thirty, found Socrates guilty. Plato writes that if just 30 votes had gone the other way, Socrates would have been acquitted. He died in prison by drinking poison. The line about the unexamined life comes from Plato’s Apology. Athenian democracy put its most famous philosopher to death.
Vote not guilty
You lose. Whenever anyone asks how you voted that day, you can answer without looking away.
Vote guilty
Your side wins. But when you hear how calmly he drank the poison, you lie awake for many nights.
The grove of Academus
Outside the walls, in an olive grove called the Academy, a broad-shouldered man named Plato teaches that everything we see is only shadows on a cave wall; the real things are elsewhere.

Plato founded the Academy around 387 BCE. The name came from the hero Academus and became our word academy. The sign over the door, “Let no one ignorant of geometry enter”, is reported by writers more than seven hundred years after Plato ✦. Plato took at least two women as pupils.
Ask about your own shadow
Plato answers at such length that the sun sets. You understand half of it, but that half stays with you for life.
Say you prefer the shadows
A pupil named Aristotle laughs out loud, then quickly looks serious.
A lamp at noon
A ragged man who sleeps in a huge clay jar walks through the noon sun holding a lamp. He shines it in everyone’s face and says he is looking for a human being. People call him Diogenes the Dog.

Diogenes (about 404–323 BCE) was a Cynic philosopher, from the Greek word for “dog”. He believed people should live simply and naturally, caring nothing for money or reputation. The lamp story and nearly all his anecdotes come from a book written some five hundred years after him ✦. Asked where he came from, he said, “I am a citizen of the world.”
Let him shine it in your face
He looks for a long time, then shakes his head: “Nearly.” You cannot decide whether to be pleased or hurt.
Give him a loaf of bread
He takes it without thanks and shares half with a dog by the road.
Stand out of my sun

A young king from Macedon named Alexander comes to Corinth. Everyone rushes to bow, except Diogenes, lying in the sun. Alexander goes to him and asks what he would like. Diogenes answers: “Stand a little out of my sun.”

Plutarch says Alexander replied, “If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes” ✦. Alexander was about twenty. The next year he began the march that would conquer Persia and reach India. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, the same year as Diogenes.
Laugh out loud
The Macedonian guards turn to look at you, but the king is laughing too, and you get away with it.
Bow properly to the king
Alexander does not notice you at all. His eyes are on the east.
The teacher who walks as he teaches

At the Lyceum a man named Aristotle paces up and down a covered walk as he teaches. On a table lies an octopus cut in half. He says dolphins breathe with lungs and bear live young like cows: they are not fish.

Aristotle opened the Lyceum in 335 BCE. His pupils were called Peripatetics, perhaps from the covered walk, perhaps from his habit of walking as he taught ✦. He wrote about more than five hundred kinds of animals, often rightly, as with dolphins, sometimes wrongly, as when he said women have fewer teeth than men. He had once been tutor to Alexander the Great.
Count your mother’s teeth
The same number as your father’s. You tell Aristotle; he notes it down but does not change his book.
Help dissect the octopus
Your hands stink for three days, but now you know an octopus has more than one heart.
On the banks of the Hyphasis

For eight years you have marched behind Alexander from Greece through Persia and Egypt to India. It has rained for seventy days and every sandal has rotted. Alexander wants to cross the river and go on, but an old officer named Coenus stands up and says, for everyone, that it is enough.

In 326 BCE, at the Hyphasis (today’s Beas in India), Alexander’s soldiers refused to go on. According to the historian Arrian, Coenus spoke for the army. Alexander shut himself in his tent for three days before agreeing to turn back. Coenus died a few days later. Alexander’s conquests spread the Greek language as far as Afghanistan and India.
Shout your agreement with Coenus
Marched to India with Alexander
The soldiers weep with joy at the news of home, but the road back across the desert will kill more men than all the battles.
Keep quiet in case the king is angry
Three days later Alexander builds twelve altars by the river and gives the order to turn back.
The Garden of Epicurus

In a vegetable garden behind a house, a man named Epicurus eats bread and water with his friends. Women and slaves sit among them, talking philosophy. He says there is no need to fear the gods or death: happiness is freedom from pain, and friends.

Epicurus founded his school, the Garden, in Athens around 306 BCE, and accepted women and slaves as pupils, which was very rare at the time. He taught that “death is nothing to us”: while we exist, death is not here, and when death is here, we no longer exist. Today “epicurean” means someone who loves fine food, the opposite of how he actually lived.
Sit and share the bread
No one asks who you are, where you come from, or whether you are a slave.
Ask whether there is any cheese
Epicurus laughs, passes a little pot of cheese, and says, “This is my feast.”
The man who reached the frozen sea

A sea captain named Pytheas comes back from a voyage to the north. He tells of an island where the sun does not set in summer, of tides as high as a two-storey house, and beyond that a sea that is neither water nor land, like a jellyfish.

Pytheas of Massalia sailed round Britain around 325 BCE and wrote of a northern land called Thule. His book is lost; we know it from later writers, many of whom called him a liar. Yet what he described, such as the midnight sun and great tides, matches the real North Sea. His “jellyfish sea” may have been forming sea ice or sea fog.
Believe him
You dream of the jellyfish sea for years.
Laugh that he is making it up
Two thousand years later, people who go there will find he was telling the truth.
No royal road

At the Library of Alexandria a teacher named Euclid draws triangles on a sand board. King Ptolemy complains it is too hard and asks whether there is a shortcut. Euclid answers: “There is no royal road to geometry.”

Euclid’s Elements (about 300 BCE) may be the longest-used textbook in the world: students still learned from it into the 20th century. The “royal road” story comes from a writer some seven hundred years later, and another version gives the words to a different mathematician speaking to Alexander the Great ✦.
Try the proof yourself
Three days later you have it. Euclid says, “Good. Now the next one.” There are more than four hundred.
Ask what use it is
Euclid tells a slave, “Give him a coin, since he must make a profit from what he learns.” ✦
The Earth goes round the Sun

An astronomer from Samos named Aristarchus measures the Moon’s shadow and concludes that the Sun is far bigger than the Earth. A big thing should not circle a small one, he says, so it is the Earth that goes round the Sun. Everyone laughs.

Aristarchus (about 310–230 BCE) proposed that the Earth goes round the Sun, almost two thousand years before Copernicus. His book on it is lost; we know of it because Archimedes mentioned it. Most people did not believe him: if the Earth moved, the stars should shift, and to the naked eye they do not, because they are far more distant than anyone imagined.
Everyone thinks you are mad. You do not care. That night you feel the ground racing under your feet.
Laugh with the others
In two thousand years, people will laugh back at all of you.
Measuring the world

The head of the Library, Eratosthenes, has heard that at Syene in the south, at noon on midsummer’s day, the sun shines straight down to the bottom of a well. On the same day in Alexandria a pillar still casts a shadow. He asks you to help measure its angle.

Eratosthenes (about 276–194 BCE) found the shadow at Alexandria was about one-fiftieth of a circle. Multiplying by the distance to Syene (today’s Aswan) gave a circumference of about 250,000 stadia. No one knows exactly how long his stadion was, but his figure was probably off by between a few percent and about 15%. Educated Greeks had known the Earth was round since Aristotle.
Measure the shadow carefully
Helped measure the size of the Earth
The angle is tiny, but multiplied out, the world is bigger than you ever imagined.
Ask who paced out the distance
He says the king’s pacers. You wonder how much their feet hurt.
Eureka

A naked man runs down a street in Syracuse shouting “Eureka, eureka!”: “I have found it!” People say it is Archimedes. In the bath he has just worked out how to prove whether the king’s gold crown was mixed with silver.

The bath story comes from Vitruvius, a Roman writer nearly two hundred years after Archimedes ✦. But Archimedes really did write a book on floating bodies, and the rule that an object in water is pushed up by the weight of the water it displaces is still called Archimedes’ principle.
Run to bring him a cloak
He ignores the cloak, grabs your arm and explains the overflowing water until you understand.
Laugh until your sides ache
The whole city laughs for years, and people go on telling it for two thousand more.
Do not disturb my circles

For two years the Roman army has besieged Syracuse. Archimedes’ machines have lifted Roman ships out of the water and tipped them over. But tonight, during a festival, Roman soldiers climb over the wall.

Syracuse fell in 212 BCE. The general Marcellus ordered that Archimedes be spared, but a soldier killed him. Legend says he was drawing geometry in the sand and told the soldier, “Do not disturb my circles” ✦. The ship-lifting machines are described by the historian Polybius; the mirrors that burned ships are a later legend ✦.
Flee to the cellar
At dawn you hear that the old man who drew circles in the sand has been killed.
Run to warn Archimedes
A sword cuts your arm before you get there.
You arrive too late. All that is left are circles in the sand, trampled to nothing.
The first race
On the meadow by the river at Olympia young men race the length of one stadion, about 190 metres. The winner is a cook from Elis named Koroibos. His prize is an olive branch.

Greeks counted years from the first Olympics in 776 BCE, and the list of victors begins with Koroibos, but the list was compiled centuries later, so historians are not sure of the date ✦. At first there was just one event, a short sprint. The word stadium comes from stadion.
Cheer yourself hoarse
He flashes past so fast you hear only bare feet on the earth.
Ask how a cook runs so fast
He laughs that he has spent his life chasing goats that escaped from the kitchen.
The farmer-poet

At a poetry contest in Chalcis a farmer from the village of Ascra, named Hesiod, wins a bronze tripod. He recites verses on the farm work of each season, and teaches that those who work hard need not go hungry.

Hesiod lived around 700 BCE. In Works and Days he tells us himself that he won a tripod at Chalcis, and grumbles about a brother who cheated him of his inheritance: one of the first times in European literature that a poet speaks of his own life.
Memorise his verses on ploughing time
“When you hear the crane calling from the clouds, it is time to plough.” You set your seasons by it all your life.
Ask about his brother
He complains for longer than the poem.
The soldier who threw away his shield

A mercenary from Paros named Archilochus sits drinking at the harbour and sings a song of his own about throwing away his shield to run from a battle. To hell with it, he sings; he can buy another. Everyone gapes.

Archilochus (about 680–645 BCE) was among the first Greek poets to write of his own feelings rather than heroes. The Spartans were said to have banned his shield poem ✦. Another famous line, “The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing”, is his too.
Laugh and sing along
The grown-ups scold you, but the whole harbour sings it for months.
Tell him he has no honour
He makes up three lines mocking you on the spot. Everyone remembers them except you.
The singer and the dolphin

At the court of Periander, ruler of Corinth, the singer Arion tells how the sailors meant to kill him for his money. He asked to sing one last song, leapt into the sea, and a dolphin carried him ashore.

Herodotus tells the story of Arion and the dolphin ✦. Periander ruled Corinth around 627–587 BCE; some counted him among the Seven Sages, others called him a cruel tyrant. In this age a “tyrant” simply meant someone who seized power rather than inheriting it, not necessarily a wicked one.
Believe the dolphin story
Every time you see dolphins after that, you sing to them.
Ask what happened to the sailors
Periander smiles coldly and says, “They were caught.” You do not ask more.
The law for drunks
Pittacus, chosen by the people of Mytilene to rule and end their civil strife, makes a new law: anyone who commits a crime while drunk is punished twice as hard as if sober.

Aristotle mentions this law of Pittacus, explaining that drunks cause more trouble, so the law looked to the public good rather than sympathy for the drunk. Pittacus was one of the Seven Sages, and stepped down of his own accord after ten years, rare for rulers in any age.
The city’s parties grow suddenly quieter, and the wine-sellers grumble.
Say drunks deserve sympathy
Pittacus replies, “Sympathy does not mend a broken head.”
The slave who tells fables

An odd-looking slave tells stories to the children at the harbour: the fox and the sour grapes, the tortoise and the hare. Every one ends with a lesson that makes the listening grown-ups blush. His name is Aesop.

Herodotus says Aesop was a slave on Samos, near Miletus, around 600 BCE. Almost everything else about his life is legend ✦, and many fables under his name were written centuries later. Aesop’s fables have been read by generations of Thai children.
Beg for another story
He tells of the ant and the cicada, glancing at his master lounging in the shade.
Ask why someone so clever is still a slave
He answers with the fable of the wolf and the collared dog. You think about it for days.
The first map of the world

Thales’ pupil Anaximander draws a map of the whole world as he imagines it: a circle, with our sea in the middle and Ocean all around. He says the Earth floats in the middle of everything with nothing holding it up.

Later Greek writers say Anaximander (about 610–546 BCE) was the first to dare draw a map of the world. His idea that the Earth hangs unsupported was a huge leap. He also suggested that the first humans came from creatures living in water.
Find your home on the map
Your home is a tiny dot beside the sea. For the first time you see how big the world is.
Ask why the Earth does not fall
He says there is no reason for it to fall one way rather than another. Your head spins all day.
Athena in a chariot
A chariot drives into the city carrying a very tall woman in the armour of Athena. Heralds cry that the goddess herself is bringing Peisistratus back to rule Athens. Many people kneel.

Herodotus says the woman was named Phye, a village woman about 1.8 metres tall, and grumbles that it was the silliest trick he ever heard of ✦. Peisistratus ruled Athens as tyrant several times between about 561 and 527 BCE, and is said to have had Homer’s poems written down ✦.
Kneel with the others
Years later you hear that the goddess sells garlands in the market.
Shout, “That’s Phye the flower-seller!”
People around you laugh, but Peisistratus’ guards remember your face.
Ten new tribes

Cleisthenes announces that Athenians will no longer be grouped by the old noble clans. Every village is reorganised into ten tribes, each mixing people from the city, the coast and the hills, and each sends fifty men to the council.

Cleisthenes’ reforms of 508–507 BCE are usually counted as the start of Athenian democracy. Mixing the tribes made it harder for noble families to control the votes of their home districts. Athenians began to add their village’s name to their own instead of their clan’s.
Go and register in your village
Now your tribesmen include hill people you had never met.
Grumble that the old ways were better
The elders of the old clans agree with you, but no one listens to them any more.
Poets at court
Hiero, ruler of Syracuse, invites the finest poets of the Greek world to his palace: Pindar, who writes songs for athletic victors, and Aeschylus, the playwright from Athens.

Pindar wrote an ode for Hiero’s horse-race victory at Olympia in 476 BCE, and Aeschylus came to Sicily more than once and died there in 456 BCE. Legend says an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head ✦.
Listen to Pindar sing
“Best of all things is water,” he begins, while everyone at the feast is drinking wine.
Ask Aeschylus whether he really fought
He is silent a long time, then tells of his brother, whose hand was cut off at Marathon.
Zeus in the workshop

At Olympia, in a workshop behind the temple, a sculptor named Phidias is building a seated Zeus so tall his head nearly touches the roof, with skin of ivory and robes of gold. An assistant hands him a clay cup of water.

The statue of Zeus at Olympia stood about 12–13 metres tall, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world; it is entirely lost. In the 1950s archaeologists excavated Phidias’ workshop, finding clay moulds for shaping the gold and a small cup inscribed underneath: “I belong to Pheidias.”
Help wash the cups
You wash the little cup with his name on it, not knowing it will be dug up two thousand four hundred years later.
Ask what happens if Zeus stands up
Phidias laughs that the roof would come off. Later writers made the same complaint.
The woman who won at Olympia

At Olympia the herald calls the winner of the four-horse chariot race: Kyniska, princess of Sparta. She is not at the track, since married women may not enter, but the horses are hers, and she chose and trained them herself.

Kyniska won the chariot race at Olympia in 396 and 392 BCE, the first woman in the list of Olympic victors. In chariot racing the owner of the horses, not the driver, was the winner. The inscription from the base of her statue at Olympia survives.
Cheer for her
Some of the men scowl, but her horses were faster than all of theirs.
Wonder whether women will ever compete themselves
In a little over two thousand years, women will compete at the Olympics for the first time.
The play called The Clouds

In Aristophanes’ comedy an actor in a Socrates mask hangs in a basket in mid-air, explaining nonsense about gnats humming through their bottoms. The whole theatre roars, and then the real Socrates stands up in the audience.

The Clouds was staged in 423 BCE and mocked Socrates as a teacher of trick arguments. In Plato’s Apology Socrates says the play turned people against him years before his trial. The story that he stood up so the audience could compare his face with the mask comes from a later writer ✦.
Turn to look at the real Socrates
The mask is such a good likeness that you laugh louder than anyone. Socrates laughs too.
Do not laugh: it seems cruel
Beside you, a young man named Plato is not laughing either.
The night of the broken gods

This morning the city wakes to find the stone pillars of the god Hermes outside every house smashed in the face, just as Athens’ greatest fleet is about to sail against Sicily. Rumour blames the rich young men around Alcibiades.

The smashing of the herms in 415 BCE remains a mystery. Alcibiades, one of the generals of the Sicilian expedition, was recalled to stand trial but fled to Sparta. The expedition ended in disaster in 413: thousands died or were sold as slaves in the stone quarries of Syracuse.
Help mend the pillar by your door
Hermes’ new nose is a little crooked, but he will probably not mind.
Go to watch the fleet sail
Alcibiades stands on deck, handsome and sure of himself. You do not know it is the last he will see of Athens for years.
The orator from Leontini

Gorgias, a teacher of speaking from a nearby city, proves before a crowd that Helen of Troy was innocent, then proves that nothing exists, and that if anything did, it could not be known. People applaud, unsure what they are applauding.

Gorgias of Leontini in Sicily was one of the most famous sophists. In 427 BCE he went as an envoy to Athens and dazzled the Athenians with his speaking. His Encomium of Helen survives, and Plato named a dialogue after him.
Pay for lessons
You become a far better speaker and win an argument with your mother for the first time. Just once.
Ask whether, if nothing exists, his fees do
The crowd laughs. Gorgias smiles and says that is an excellent question, at double the price.
A philosopher for sale

A philosopher from Athens named Plato has come to teach Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, that a good ruler must be a philosopher. Dionysius is not pleased at all. Rumour says he has had Plato sold as a slave.

Diogenes Laertius says Plato was sold into slavery after quarrelling with Dionysius I, and a friend had to ransom him ✦. Plato went back to Syracuse twice more to try to create a “philosopher-king”, and failed every time.
Go to the slave market to see
A broad-shouldered man stands still on the block, begging no one. A buyer asks what he can do. He says, “Govern men.”
Keep quiet; do not cross the tyrant
In Syracuse people have learned to whisper.
Pebbles in the mouth
On the beach a skinny young man fills his mouth with pebbles and shouts against the roar of the waves. People say his name is Demosthenes, and that the assembly once laughed at his stammer.

Plutarch says Demosthenes trained by speaking with pebbles in his mouth over the noise of the waves ✦. He became Athens’ greatest orator and spent his life urging the Athenians to resist Philip of Macedon. His speeches gave us the word philippic, a fierce verbal attack.
Try speaking with pebbles yourself
You nearly swallow one. Demosthenes mumbles, “Careful.”
Listen to him rehearse against Philip
In the end his voice is louder than the waves, and you want to go to war at once.
The man who counts fish

At the salt lagoon on Lesbos a foreigner named Aristotle and his friend Theophrastus wade about all day, writing down where octopuses lay their eggs and what sea urchins eat, and questioning every fisherman who passes.

Aristotle lived on Lesbos around 345–344 BCE, and much of the sea life in his books comes from the lagoon of Pyrrha there. Some modern biologists call Lesbos the birthplace of biology. Theophrastus later wrote one of the world’s first books on plants.
Show him where the fish spawn
He writes down every word you say and asks questions no fisherman in the village ever thought of.
Sell him an octopus
He does not eat it but cuts it open on a table. What a waste, you think.
The woman philosopher

A woman of a rich family named Hipparchia has left home to live like Diogenes with her husband Crates, sleeping in the street and arguing with male philosophers at dinners. A man sneers that she should go back to her loom. She answers that the time she did not spend weaving, she spent on learning: what is wrong with that?
Diogenes Laertius records Hipparchia and her reply. She is one of the few Greek women philosophers whose names we know, along with women who studied with Plato and Epicurus.
Applaud her
Some of the men glare at you, but she smiles at you.
Ask whether she fears the gossip
She laughs: “If I feared gossip, I would still be at my loom.”
The Painted Porch

Under the painted colonnade in the market, a shipwrecked merchant from Cyprus named Zeno teaches that we cannot control what happens to us, only our own minds. Poor and rich sit side by side to listen.

Zeno began teaching at the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch in the Athenian agora, around 300 BCE, so his followers were called Stoics: our word stoic, calm in hardship. Centuries later the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius belonged to this school.
Sit and listen every day
The next year, when your field floods, you are less angry than you expected.
Ask about his shipwreck
He says the shipwreck was the luckiest thing in his life, because it brought him here.
The king’s procession

King Ptolemy’s procession passes through the city all day: carriages drawn by elephants, lions, leopards, parrots, a great white bear, a giant wine vat spilling into the street, and tens of thousands of soldiers marching behind.

The Grand Procession of Ptolemy II in Alexandria, around the 270s BCE, was described by an eyewitness and preserved in a book by Athenaeus. The list includes elephants, many African animals and a white bear, whose origin scholars still puzzle over.
Climb onto a roof to watch
You count twenty-four elephants before you give up counting.
Go and catch wine from the giant vat
Your cloak is purple all over, and you remember nothing of the end of the procession.
The doctor who opens the dead

A doctor named Herophilus openly dissects human bodies, forbidden in other Greek cities. He shows you thin white cords running from the brain throughout the body, and says that thought lives in the brain, not the heart.

In early Ptolemaic Alexandria, Herophilus and Erasistratus were the first doctors to dissect human bodies systematically. Herophilus told nerves apart from tendons and showed the brain was the centre of the nervous system, whereas Aristotle had believed thought lived in the heart.
Help record what you see
You have nightmares for many nights, but know more about the human body than almost any doctor in the world.
Leave the room to be sick
He does not mind, only says his first pupil did the same.
A costly victory

King Pyrrhus of Epirus arrives with war elephants to help Syracuse fight Carthage. His soldiers say he has just beaten the Romans in Italy, but lost so many men that Pyrrhus grumbled, “One more victory like that and we are finished.”

Plutarch reports Pyrrhus’ words after his battle with Rome in 279 BCE ✦, which gave us the phrase “Pyrrhic victory”: a win so costly it amounts to a loss. Pyrrhus campaigned in Sicily in 278–276 BCE before returning to Italy and losing to Rome.
Go and see the elephants
An elephant tugs your cloak with its trunk. The soldiers say it likes you. You are not so sure.
Ask why he keeps fighting if winning means losing
An old soldier laughs: “Because he is a king, and kings never know when to stop.”
Burning the debts
A young king named Agis orders every debt contract in Sparta piled in the market and burned. Next, he promises, the land will be shared out equally again, as in the old days.

In the Hellenistic age Sparta’s land fell into the hands of a few families, and fewer than a thousand citizens remained. Agis IV burned the debt records around 242 BCE but was executed the next year, before the land could be shared. Cleomenes III carried the reform through around 227 BCE, but lost a war in 222 and it collapsed.
Throw a contract on the fire
The papyrus burns faster than you expected. Three generations of debt go up in a single puff of smoke.
Watch, wondering how long it will last
The next year you have your answer.
The freedom of the Greeks

At the Isthmian Games outside the city, a Roman general named Flamininus has the herald proclaim that all the Greek cities are free: no foreign garrisons, no tribute. The crowd roars so loudly that nobody watches the games any more.

Flamininus proclaimed “the freedom of the Greeks” in 196 BCE, after Rome defeated Macedon. Plutarch says the shout was so loud that birds flying overhead fell from the sky ✦. Fifty years later the Romans came back and burned Corinth, a few kilometres away.
Cheer for Rome
You are hoarse for three days, and believe the world has truly changed.
Wonder why a foreigner must proclaim our freedom
An old man beside you nods slowly: “What can be given can be taken back.”
The hero’s urn

A funeral procession passes through the village. A young man named Polybius carries the urn holding the ashes of Philopoemen, the last Arcadian general the Greeks honoured, so covered with garlands it can barely be seen.

Plutarch says Polybius carried Philopoemen’s urn in 183 BCE. Polybius, from Megalopolis in Arcadia, was later taken to Rome as a hostage, befriended Roman generals and saw Carthage destroyed with his own eyes. His history set out to explain how Rome came to rule the world.
Walk with the procession
Polybius glances at you once, with the look of a man memorising everything to write down later.
Scatter flowers
Your flowers land right on the urn.
“Fish and beasts devour one another, for they have no justice; but to mankind Zeus gave justice.”
Hesiod, the farmer-poet, about 700 BCE
“I wrote laws alike for the base and the noble, fitting straight justice to each.”
Solon, lawgiver of Athens, 594 BCE
“Laws are like spiders’ webs: they hold the weak and small, but the rich and powerful tear right through.”
Anacharsis the Scythian to Solon, as Plutarch tells it ✦
“The people must fight for the law as for their city wall.”
Heraclitus of Ephesus, about 500 BCE
“There are unwritten, unfailing laws, higher than any ruler’s decree.”
Antigone, in Sophocles’ play, 441 BCE
“A man who takes no interest in public affairs we call not quiet, but useless.”
Pericles, in Thucydides, 431 BCE
“The law is reason free from desire.”
Aristotle, in the Politics
“Always be the best, and stand above the rest.”
Homer’s Iliad
“Observe due measure: moderation is best in all things.”
Hesiod, Works and Days
“Know thyself.”
inscribed at the temple of Delphi
“Nothing in excess.”
“Call no man happy until he is dead.”
Solon to King Croesus, as Herodotus tells it ✦
“No one steps into the same river twice.”
Heraclitus, as Plato reports him
“Man is the measure of all things.”
Protagoras, the teacher of rhetoric
“The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.”
Socrates, in Plato’s Apology, 399 BCE
“Help, or at least do no harm.”
the books of the Hippocratic school
“I am a citizen of the world.”
Diogenes ✦
“Death is nothing to us.”
Chose a saying to live by
The sea that poured in
Grandfather points west, where the sun sets, and tells how at the end of the world the hero Heracles split a mountain in two, and the water of the Ocean poured in to make our sea.

Greek legend called the two sides of the Strait of Gibraltar the Pillars of Heracles ✦. The geology is more astonishing. About 6 million years ago the channels to the Atlantic closed and the Mediterranean evaporated almost dry, leaving salt basins kilometres deep. About 5.3 million years ago the ocean burst back in through the strait. One model suggests most of the water arrived in less than two years, hundreds of times the flow of the Amazon, with the sea rising by up to about 10 metres a day. Geologists still debate how fast it really was.
Ask what was here before
Grandfather laughs and says only rocks and salt, probably. You have no idea how right he is.
Ask whether you could walk to the pillars
Grandfather says it is many days by ship, and beyond the pillars is only Ocean, from which no one comes back to tell.
Frogs round a pond

You climb the hill behind the house. Whichever way you look you see sea, islands and mountains. Every bay has its own little town, with its own rulers, gods and laws, and every town thinks it matters most.

The sea reaches into Greece from every side, and mountains split the land into small valleys, with no great plain one king could easily rule. So Greeks lived in poleis, small city-states: historians count more than a thousand. Plato wrote that the Greeks lived round the sea “like ants or frogs round a pond”. Divided as they were, they spoke one language, worshipped the same gods and competed together at Olympia.
Count the towns you can see
You count seven, and know that three of them are enemies of yours.
Sing to the frogs
The frogs in the pool croak back. You think they probably believe their pond is the whole world too.
The anger of Achilles
At a feast a blind bard recites the war at Troy all night long without looking at anything. You are sleepy but refuse to sleep, because you want to know whether Hector survives.

The Iliad and the Odyssey were probably composed in the 8th or 7th century BCE, from poems memorised and passed on for centuries before being written down. Scholars still argue whether “Homer” was one poet or many. Greek children learned to read from his verses, and some could recite them entire. The blind Homer is a legend ✦.
Recite along
You remember thirty lines, and the grown-ups applaud.
Ask why the gods quarrel like people
The bard laughs: “Because people are the ones telling it.”
The boy-leader
Every morning the family’s old slave walks you to school, carrying your lyre and wax tablet, and taps you with a stick if you dawdle. One teacher teaches letters, another the lyre, another wrestling.
The slave who took a boy to school was the paidagogos, which became the English word pedagogue. Schools charged fees: most poor boys got only a few years or none, and most girls learned at home.
Talk with the old slave on the way
He was a farmer’s son in Thrace before he was captured and sold. He tells of his homeland better than the teacher tells Homer.
Run off to play at the harbour
The old slave puffs after you and catches up, and then your father scolds him instead of you.
Seven years old

On your seventh birthday you are taken from home to live with the other boys your age. You get one cloak for the whole year, go barefoot, sleep on reeds you pull from the river yourself, and are fed so little that you must steal.

The Spartan training system was the agoge. Boys were taught to steal food without being caught; if caught they were whipped, not for stealing but for clumsiness. The tale of the boy who hid a fox cub under his cloak and let it bite him to death without a sound comes from Plutarch ✦.
Steal cheese from the altar
You are caught and whipped. The other boys look on with contempt, not pity.
No one sees. That night you share the cheese with your group.
Endure the hunger
You grow thin enough to count your ribs, but the trainer gives you a nod.
A saying to live by

In the square people quote the wise to argue about everything, from the price of olive oil to war. Your teacher says a good person should have one saying to hold to all their life. Which do you choose?

Greeks loved collecting sayings. At Delphi short precepts were inscribed for all to read, and Greeks honoured the “Seven Sages”, each with sayings of his own on law, government and how to live. Many Greek sayings are still quoted in law courts, medical schools and on classroom walls, though some are stories whose real speaker is uncertain ✦.
The dowry

Your father has arranged your marriage. The groom is about thirty; you have seen his face once. Your father sets aside a dowry of silver and woven cloth that goes with you; if he divorces you, he must give it all back.
Your family and a neighbouring family discuss a marriage. The bride is fourteen; her family will give a dowry of silver and ten olive trees.

In Athens women usually married at about 14–15, to men of about 30. Marriages were arranged by a father or male guardian. Women could not own land or make large contracts themselves; the dowry was their security. In Sparta women married later and could hold land.
The wedding procession goes by night, with torches, songs and a cart carrying the bride to her new home.
The elders grumble, but agree to wait.
A young soldier
You are old enough for military training: two years guarding the border forts, and an oath to the gods never to desert the man beside you in the line.

Greek infantry were called hoplites, perhaps after the big round shield. Each man bought his own armour. Each shield covered half its bearer and half the man beside him, so throwing away your shield was the worst disgrace. The oath of young Athenian soldiers survives on a 4th-century BCE inscription.
Swear in a loud voice
Your voice is louder than anyone’s, and you are embarrassed all day.
Swear quietly, but remember every word
You can still recite that oath when you are old.
The ships to the colony

There is not enough land for everyone. Your city asked the god at Delphi, and the answer was to send people to found a new city across the sea to the west. The leader is looking for young people bold enough to go.

Between about 750 and 550 BCE Greeks founded hundreds of colonies from Spain to the Black Sea. Southern Italy had so many Greek cities that the Romans called it Magna Graecia, “Great Greece”. Many are still inhabited, such as Marseille, Naples and Istanbul. Colonies were independent cities, not ruled by their mother city.
Take ship
The ships carry you to found a little town on a coast no one has heard of.
You cross the sea to start again in a town that is still only a few houses and an altar.
Many ships sail. Some never come back.
Ostracism day
This year the assembly has voted to hold an ostracism. Everyone brings a potsherd to write the name of the politician they want out of the city for ten years. Whoever gets the most must go.

Ostracism was not a criminal punishment: the exile kept his property and could return after ten years. It was used from about 487 to 417 BCE. The last time is known to have misfired, when two rival politicians joined forces to have a third man exiled instead; after that it was never used again.
Write the most powerful man’s name
He gets only a few hundred votes and stays.
Do not vote
Your neighbours call you “useless”, half joking.
The allotment machine

This morning you slot your bronze name-ticket into a great stone slab. An official drops black and white balls down a tube: white means your row serves on a jury today. The case: two neighbours quarrelling over a goat.

Athenians chose jurors at random with a stone allotment machine, the kleroterion, so no one could bribe a jury in advance. Jurors were paid half a drachma a day. A court had hundreds of jurors, no judge and no lawyers: everyone spoke for himself.
Listen carefully to both sides
The goat goes back to the one who speaks less well but more truly.
Doze off in court
You wake in time to vote and are paid your half-drachma like everyone else.
The resident foreigner

You were born in this city, pay taxes and go to war when called, but your family came from elsewhere three generations ago. So you are still a “resident foreigner”: you cannot buy a house or land, and need a citizen sponsor to go to court.

In Athens resident foreigners were called metics. They paid a yearly tax of 12 drachmas for a man and 6 for a woman. After a law of 451 BCE, only those with an Athenian father and mother could be citizens. Many famous thinkers and businessmen, Aristotle among them, were metics all their lives.
Get rich in business instead
Money cannot buy citizenship, but it buys a little respect.
Make close friends among the citizens
A friend takes you into feasts where no one asks where you are from.
For years you have saved every coin your owner gave you as a reward, until you almost have enough to buy yourself. At Delphi a slave can be “sold” to the god Apollo, who then sets them free.

The walls at Delphi carry more than a thousand inscriptions recording the freeing of slaves. Most slaves paid for their own freedom, and many still had to serve their former owner until the owner died. Slaves in the silver mines at Laurion had almost no such chance; some worked in tunnels less than a metre high.
Pay everything you have
Your name is carved on the stone wall. You are free, though still a foreigner without citizen rights.
Your owner raises the price, saying you are worth more than that.
Save a few more years
Every coin you get, you hide in a crack in the wall.
The women’s festival

For three days in autumn the married women of the city camp on a hill and hold rites for the goddess Demeter. Men may not come near. Everyone eats, laughs and says things they would never say in front of their husbands.

The Thesmophoria was one of the few festivals where Greek women gathered by themselves, without men. Its rites were kept so secret that we know very little. A male comic playwright wrote a comedy about a man who dresses as a woman to sneak in.
Join every rite
You come home hoarse, and smile for a week.
Listen to the old women’s stories
You learn more of the city’s secrets than all the men in the assembly know.
The drinking party

At a party where everyone reclines on couches, the host orders the wine mixed with three parts water. One man recites verses, another argues about love, then everyone plays the game of flicking the dregs of their cups at a target.

Greeks thought drinking unmixed wine was barbarian. The drinking party was the symposion, origin of the English word symposium. The game of flicking wine at a target was kottabos. Women at these parties were usually musicians or paid companions, not the guests’ wives.
Play kottabos
Your wine splashes the next guest’s cloak, and the whole room laughs.
Join the argument about love
You speak so well someone writes it down. In the morning you cannot remember what you said.
The drama festival

The whole city stops work for the open-air theatre: three tragedies from morning to evening, then a comedy mocking the politicians sitting in the front row. Every actor is a man in a mask, even in women’s roles.

Greek drama grew from festivals for the god Dionysus; the word tragedy may come from “goat song”. The theatre at Epidaurus held about 13,000–14,000 people, and a whisper on stage can still be heard in the back row. Later Athens had a fund that paid poor citizens’ tickets.
Weep at the tragedies
You go home with swollen eyes, but feeling light, as if washed clean.
Laugh at the comedy
The politicians in the front row turn crimson, and the whole theatre laughs until the stone seats shake.
The books on the ships
The king’s officials search every ship that docks. Any book they find is taken to the Library to be copied and returned, though sometimes they return the copy and keep the original.

The Library of Alexandria may have held tens or even hundreds of thousands of scrolls. The story of seizing books from ships comes from the physician Galen ✦. The Library was not burned in a single day: it declined over centuries through fire, war and lack of money.
Help copy the books
You copy a play no one has read, and that no one will read again in a thousand years.
Hide your book under the fish jars
The officials have no wish to reach into the salt-fish jars. Your book is safe.
Zeus or Jupiter?

A Roman trader sits drinking in the market square, points at the statue of the god and says, “Our Jupiter is better than your Zeus.” You reply that they are the same god. He insists not: the names are different. The whole market starts taking sides.

Both are half right. Greek “Zeus” and Latin “Jupiter” come from the same ancient word, reconstructed by linguists as *Dyēus, “sky”. Jupiter comes from “sky-god + father”; Greeks too called him “Zeus the father”, and India’s Vedas call the sky god Dyaus Pitar: the very same phrase. The Romans borrowed many Greek stories, but Rome’s own gods kept rites and characters of their own.
Shout “Zeus pater!”
The Roman shouts back, “Iuppiter!” Both sides hoot until the innkeeper pours free wine to quiet them. By the end everyone is swearing by the same name without noticing.
Say the god surely doesn’t care what we call him
The Roman is silent a long while, then raises his cup to you: “To the father of the sky, whatever his name.”
The words of a lifetime
Say you still believe it
The child repeats it and runs to tell friends, as you once did.
Say life taught you something different
The child asks what. It takes you all afternoon to answer.
Signing the vase
This vase is the best you have ever painted: Achilles and Ajax playing a board game in the middle of the war. Will you write your own name on it?

Some Greek vase painters signed their work “... painted me”. Exekias painted Achilles and Ajax at a board game around 530 BCE, on a vase now in the Vatican Museums. Around the same time Athenian workshops began switching from black figures on red to red figures on black.
Sign it
Leave it unsigned: let the picture speak
Two thousand years later, scholars will name you by your style, something like “the Achilles Painter”.
One stroke
In the trireme you sit in the dark of the lowest bank, your head below the seat of the man above, his sweat dripping on you. If anyone misses the stroke, a whole row of oars clashes.

In 1987 the Greek navy built a reconstructed trireme, the Olympias. Volunteer crews reached about 9 knots, showing how hard ancient rowers must have trained. Most Athenian rowers were poor citizens and paid foreigners, not the chained slaves of the movies.
Sing to keep the stroke
The whole bank sings along and the ship leaps forward until the captain laughs.
Row in silence, saving strength
You are the only one with strength left when you reach port.
The city physician
A small town offers you a salary to be its public physician, treating everyone who falls sick, rich or poor. But if anyone dies, the family will blame you.

Some Greek cities paid public physicians from taxes. Hippocratic books taught doctors to record a patient’s symptoms day by day and to say plainly when they could not cure. One book records 42 cases, and more than half the patients died.
You see every illness there is, and write everything down.
Better to treat only the rich
You grow rich fast, but you never see anything new.
Teaching for pay
A rich father offers you a large sum to teach his son to win every debate in the assembly, whether he is right or wrong.

Travelling teachers of speaking who charged fees were called sophists. The word once meant “wise ones”, but Plato and Socrates scorned them for selling cleverness instead of truth, so that English sophistry now means deceptive argument.
Take the money
Your pupil wins his first debate with an argument you do not believe yourself.
Say you can only teach how to seek the truth
The rich father stalks off, but the son slips back to listen to you every day.
Two cities’ armies face each other on a plain, both full of farmers who need to get back for the harvest. In the shield wall everyone edges to the right, to hide behind the next man’s shield.

Hoplite battles usually ended in a single day: the front ranks shoved with their shields until one side broke. Thucydides noticed that armies drifted to the right, as each man tried to shelter behind the shield of the man on his right.
Hold your place in the line
A spear finds the gap between shields and pierces your shoulder, but the line holds.
The other side breaks first. Everyone gets home for the harvest.
Cover the man on your left
Your arm aches for a month, but the man on your left lives.

the Lydian woman
In late autumn the whole family beats the olive branches with long poles, and the olives rain down onto cloths spread beneath.

The olive was Greece’s most important crop. Its oil was eaten, burned in lamps, rubbed on the body after bathing and given as prizes. Olive trees take years to bear fruit, so an enemy who cut them down harmed a family for generations.
The north wind blows hard all month and every ship stays in harbour. The traders complain their wine will sour before it sells.
The strong summer north wind of the Aegean is the meltemi. Greeks sailed mostly in summer and hardly ever put to sea in winter.
In the agora fishmongers shout prices, a politician speaks from a stone platform, people argue about the war, and a dog runs off with an octopus.
The agora was the heart of a Greek town: market, law court, meeting place and promenade. Women of good family seldom went to market themselves; slaves or the men of the house went instead.
The family brings a cake shaped like an ox to the altar, since they cannot afford a real one.

Greeks worshipped by sacrificing animals and sharing the meat at a feast; the gods got the bones wrapped in fat, burned so the smoke rose to heaven. Myth says Prometheus tricked Zeus into choosing that share ✦. The poor offered cakes, fruit or clay animal figures instead.
Naked boys race in the gymnasium while old men sit watching and criticising everyone’s running.
The word gymnasium comes from the Greek gymnos, “naked”: Greeks trained and competed naked, and thought a well-trained body part of being a good citizen.
A seer cuts open a sheep at the rites and studies its liver. He says the gods allow the army to march, and the general smiles.
Before important decisions Greeks often read omens from the livers of sacrificed animals or from birds, or consulted the oracle at Delphi, whose answers were often ambiguous enough to read many ways.
An olive-oil lamp flickers in the room. Mother spins wool and tells of Penelope, who wove by day and secretly unpicked her work at night.
Every four years at the Panathenaia a procession the length of the city carries a new robe to Athena’s statue. Girls and women of Athens have woven it.

The procession was carved on the walls of the Parthenon. Most of the carvings were taken to Britain in the early 19th century and are in the British Museum today; Greece is still asking for them back.
An earthquake brings down almost every house in Sparta. Soon the helots across the land rise in revolt.
The great earthquake at Sparta around 464 BCE killed many people and was followed by a helot revolt that lasted years. Sparta, always afraid of the helots, grew harsher still.

In the crowded city people start running high fevers, with red eyes, coughs and a thirst so great they throw themselves into wells. Bodies pile up by the temples. No doctor can cure it, and the doctors die most of all.

The plague of Athens in 430 BCE may have killed a quarter to a third of the city, Pericles among them the next year. Thucydides caught it, survived and described it in detail. Scientists still do not know what it was; typhoid and typhus are candidates.
At night the fire atop the Pharos lighthouse shines so far that sailors see it before they see land.

The Pharos lighthouse was completed around 280 BCE and may have stood over 100 metres tall. One of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, it fell in medieval earthquakes. The word for lighthouse in several languages, such as French phare, comes from Pharos.
In the market of Alexandria you hear Greek, Egyptian, Hebrew and Aramaic all in one day.

After Alexander, Greek became the common language from Egypt to Afghanistan. The Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek at Alexandria in this period, the Septuagint, and Greek would later be the language of the New Testament.
A goatherd plays the pipes of Pan on the mountain, and the sound fills the valley.
Local people who are not Greek bring wheat and wool to trade for wine and handsome painted jars.

Greek colonies lived among native peoples: the Sikels in Sicily, the Celts around Massalia. The Celts took up Greek wine-drinking; the largest Greek bronze wine-mixing bowl known was found in the grave of a Celtic woman at Vix, in France.
Your knees ache whenever the cold wind blows. You sit in the porch listening to the children mangle their Homer.
Some young men argue that the young no longer respect their elders. You laugh, having heard the same complaint since you were a child.
Cicadas shrill in the olive trees at noon.
A donkey brays by the well.
The smell of bread and woodsmoke drifts from the ovens.
Hammers ring from the smithies all day.
Children play knucklebones in the alley.
Lyre music drifts from a house.
Women carry water jars home from the fountain.
The sea breeze carries the smell of salt to the house.
Goat bells clink on the hillside.
A little owl calls from the roof: Athena’s bird.
the plague of Athens
The winter rains never come. The streams dry up and the barley on the hillsides dies. Every household must buy grain from the Black Sea ships.
A great earthquake topples temple columns like skittles and brings the mud-brick houses down.
A winter storm lashes the coast, smashing ships in the harbour and sending roof tiles flying.
Torrential rain sends a flash flood down the ravine, sweeping away terrace walls and vines.
wounds from battle
a shipwreck
A few generations after you, the quarrelling Greek cities will band together against the Persian Empire, the largest in the world, and win.
After you, Athens and Sparta will fight each other to exhaustion; then a king from Macedon in the north will master all Greece, and his son will carry the Greek language to India.

Not long after you, Rome will swallow all of Greece. Yet Romans will learn Greek, hire Greek teachers, copy Greek statues and worship Greek gods under Latin names. A Roman poet wrote that captured Greece took her savage conqueror captive.

The English word democracy comes from Greek: “power of the people”. But in Athens those who could vote were male citizens over 18, perhaps only 10–20% of the people of the city-state. Women, slaves and foreigners had no say at all, and this democracy executed Socrates. What the Greeks left was not a finished answer, but the idea that ordinary people should share in deciding the affairs of their city, and the habit of asking why, which later generations used to extend those rights to people the Greeks themselves never counted.

Many words people around the world use today come from your language: politics, history, philosophy, mathematics, theatre, music; and the letters used to write English descend from the Greek alphabet.
In one lifetime you met
, most of whom never knew who you were, though you remembered every one of them.
The words you lived by were
On the day Athens condemned Socrates, you were one of the minority.
On the day Athens condemned Socrates, you voted with the majority.
In this game, a vase bearing your signature may still sit in some museum.
You saw the day Corinth burned, which historians often use to mark the end of independent ancient Greece.

Greeks believed the dead must be buried or burned with proper rites, or the soul would wander. The women of the family washed and dressed the body and sang laments. Sometimes a coin was placed in the mouth to pay Charon the ferryman across the river of the dead ✦. A good grave had a carved stone showing the dead person clasping hands in farewell with their family.
Put a coin in the mouth for Charon
A small coin on the tongue, enough for the crossing.
Sing laments all night
The women of the house sing until they are hoarse. Grief sung aloud weighs less than grief held in.
Hire a carver for a gravestone
On the stone he sits clasping your hand. Neither weeps, but anyone can see it is a farewell.
Your body is carried in procession to the cemetery outside the walls, with hired mourners, and a carved stone of you is set up beside the road.
You are buried in a simple grave with no name, but a fellow slave leaves a loaf of bread beside it.
Your family washes your body with olive oil and buries you with a little oil flask and a single coin.
Greeks believed the world was full of gods who quarrelled like people. If you could tell a Thai child today about one of them, which story would you tell?
In Athens only a minority could vote. In your own country today, who still has no voice?
On this vase are the people you met:
The game’s picture is only an imitation.
famous people met
drachmas
The vase of your life

At Olympia the herald calls the winner of the four-horse chariot race: Kyniska, princess of Sparta. She did not race herself, since women may not compete, but the horses are hers, and she chose and trained them herself.
Romans did not cremate babies. Your family buries your small body near the house.
One of your children falls ill and dies. Romans did not cremate babies, so the family buries the little body near the house.
the Republic: the wars with Carthage and Hannibal’s elephants
the civil wars: from the Gracchi to Caesar
the Empire at its height: the Roman peace
the late Empire: a throne for sale, plagues, and an empire split in two
Rome, the city of seven hills on the Tiber
Pompeii, the seaside town below Mount Vesuvius
Ostia, the port of Rome
Carthage, the harbour city on the African coast
Alexandria, the great port of Roman Egypt

At its height Rome may have held about a million people, more than any Western city until the 19th century. The poor lived in tall rented blocks called insulae, often without kitchens; fires were common, and the higher the floor, the cheaper the rent, because it was harder to escape.

Pompeii was a middling town of perhaps 10,000–20,000 people. Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE and buried it in ash, giving us the most detailed picture of everyday Roman life, from loaves in the ovens to the messages people scrawled on walls.

Ostia was the harbour at the mouth of the Tiber, where grain from Egypt and Africa landed to feed Rome. Its ruins still have public latrines with rows of stone seats, snack bars and warehouses to walk through today.

Carthage, founded by Phoenicians, fought Rome in three Punic Wars, was destroyed in 146 BCE, and was rebuilt as a Roman city under Julius Caesar and Augustus, becoming one of the great cities of the Empire.
After Cleopatra died in 30 BCE, Egypt belonged directly to the Roman emperor. Its wheat fed Rome, and from ports on the Red Sea Roman ships sailed to India every year on the monsoon winds.

Judaea was under Roman power from 63 BCE. Its Jewish people worshipped one God and would not worship the emperor, leading to repeated conflict with Rome until the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed in 70 CE.

Britannia was the Empire’s northernmost frontier. Its soldiers came from all over the Empire: Germans, Syrians, North Africans. The fort of Vindolanda near Hadrian’s Wall preserved letters on thin wooden tablets in its mud for well over a thousand years.
The Gauls spoke a Celtic language and drank beer, along with wine bought from Roman traders. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in 58–50 BCE; over the following centuries Latin slowly turned into French.

The emperor Constantine dedicated Constantinople as a new capital in 330 CE, on the site of the old Greek city of Byzantium. Its people spoke Greek but called themselves “Romans”, and the eastern Empire lasted another thousand years.
Most people in the Empire did not live in cities but were farmers growing wheat, olives and grapes. Many worked for great landowners, or alongside slaves on the big estates called latifundia.
Male Roman citizens had three names: a personal name, a family name and a nickname. Women usually used only the feminine form of the family name.

Upper-class Romans looked down on manual work, yet the Roman economy rested on craftsmen, slaves and freed slaves, many of whom grew rich in business. Their tombs often proudly show their trades, like the giant tomb of Eurysaces the baker at a gate of Rome.
a senatorial or equestrian family

a freed slave

Roman citizens had legal rights, such as appealing to the emperor and not being flogged without trial. Provincials lacked them, until in 212 CE the emperor Caracalla made every free person in the Empire a citizen. In Italy slaves may have been as many as a fifth of the population.
round loaves
jars of garum
The moneylender seizes the things in your rented room for the debt.
Roman moneylenders could legally charge about 12% a year, though many charged more. Brutus, Caesar’s assassin, once lent to a city in Cyprus at 48%.
A proclamation from Rome: every free person in the Empire is now a Roman citizen, you included.
In 212 CE the emperor Caracalla decreed that almost every free person in the Empire was a citizen. One Roman historian claimed the real reason was to collect inheritance tax from more people.
News from Cannae: Hannibal has surrounded and destroyed the Roman army in a single day. Women weep in every street; every household has lost someone.

At Cannae in 216 BCE perhaps 50,000 Roman soldiers died in one afternoon, one of the bloodiest days of battle in history. But Rome would not surrender, and fought on for more than a decade until it won.
Survived the day Rome destroyed Carthage
Roman soldiers fight their way in house by house. The city burns for six days, and the survivors are sold as slaves.

Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. The story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt so nothing would grow appears in no ancient source; it is a modern invention ✦. A century later Carthage was a thriving Roman city again.
Fire breaks out in the shops by the chariot track and the wind drives it on for nine days. Ten of the city’s fourteen districts are damaged, and your family sleeps in a public garden.

In the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE Nero did not fiddle ✦: the violin had not been invented, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when it began. Nero blamed the city’s small group of Christians and killed them cruelly.
This year you hear the name of a new emperor four times. The coin-makers have barely finished carving one face before they must start another.
69 CE is called the Year of the Four Emperors: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. The first three were dead within the year. Coins of each survive, some struck over the face of the one before.
Rumour says Queen Cleopatra has died in her tomb. Roman soldiers fill the streets; Egypt has no pharaoh any more.

Cleopatra died in 30 BCE. The asp bite ✦ is a story; even ancient writers were not sure. A fun fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Survived the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem
Titus’ army takes Jerusalem. The Temple is burned, all but its western wall, and thousands are carried off as slaves.

In 70 CE Rome destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem. A relief on the Arch of Titus in Rome still shows soldiers carrying off its seven-branched lampstand, and an inscription, as scholars have reconstructed it, says the Colosseum was built from war spoils. The Western Wall is still a place of Jewish prayer today.
Your family carried you out of town when the first pumice fell. You grow up in another village, hearing the grown-ups talk of the town that vanished under the ash.
Soldiers returning from the east have brought a sickness: a rash all over the body, a high fever, whole families dead.
The Antonine Plague began around 165 CE and may have killed a tenth of the Empire or more. Many scholars think it was smallpox; the physician Galen recorded its symptoms.
News arrives that the guards in Rome murdered the emperor and sold the throne to whoever paid them most. A few months later the buyer is killed too, and a frontier general marches on Rome.

In 193 CE Didius Julianus won the auction for the throne at 25,000 sesterces per soldier and reigned 66 days. That year had five emperors; Septimius Severus, a general from North Africa, came out on top.
Alaric’s Goths break into Rome: the first time in eight hundred years an enemy has sacked the city. Across the Empire no one can believe it.
In 410 CE the Goths sacked Rome for three days. A later historian tells that the emperor Honorius heard “Roma has perished” and was distraught, thinking it meant his favourite chicken, named Roma ✦.
You help unload sacks of grain from a ship and are paid in copper coins.

A first-century legionary earned about 225 denarii a year; a loaf cost a few asses (16 asses to the denarius). In the 3rd century emperors kept cutting the silver in the coins until they were almost pure copper, and prices soared.
